entries.1:1: This lists the family of Jacob who moved to Egypt. It reminds the reader that the story of Israel begins with one family.
entries.1:2: This names the first sons of Jacob. These names show that real people, not just a crowd, started the nation.
entries.1:3: More of Jacob's sons are named here. Each one became part of the family that grew into Israel.
entries.1:4: The last sons are listed. Together they make up the whole family that went to Egypt.
entries.1:5: Jacob's family totaled seventy people, and Joseph was already in Egypt. God had kept his promise to make a family from Jacob.
entries.1:6: Joseph and his brothers all died, ending that generation. Time passed, and the story moves on to their descendants.
entries.1:7: The Israelites had many children and became very numerous and strong. God was blessing them and keeping his promise to Abraham.
entries.1:8: A new king took over Egypt who did not know or care about Joseph. A leader can forget past kindnesses, so God's people must trust God more than rulers.
entries.1:9: The king told his people that the Israelites were too many and too strong. Fear of others can lead people to treat them badly.
entries.1:10: The king wanted to control the Israelites so they would not join Egypt's enemies. He acted out of fear, not fairness.
entries.1:11: Egypt forced the Israelites into hard labor and made them build cities for Pharaoh. Cruel work was meant to weaken them.
entries.1:12: The harder the Egyptians treated them, the more the Israelites grew. God blessed his people even under oppression, and the Egyptians came to hate them.
entries.1:13: The Egyptians made the Israelites work even harder. Oppression often gets worse, but God still sees his people.
entries.1:14: Their lives became bitter with making bricks and doing field work under harsh conditions. God's people suffered greatly, yet he had not forgotten them.
entries.1:15: The king spoke to two Hebrew midwives named Shiphrah and Puah. These women were given a terrible order by a powerful ruler.
entries.1:16: The king told the midwives to kill baby boys but let girls live. He wanted to stop the Israelites from growing strong.
entries.1:17: The midwives feared God and refused to kill the boys. When human orders clash with God's will, we should obey God.
entries.1:18: The king called the midwives and asked why the boys were still alive. Their courage put them in danger.
entries.1:19: The midwives told Pharaoh that Hebrew women gave birth too quickly for them to arrive. They answered cleverly while still protecting the babies.
entries.1:20: God blessed the midwives, and the Israelites kept growing stronger. God honors those who do what is right.
entries.1:21: Because the midwives feared God, he gave them families of their own. God rewards those who put him first.
entries.1:22: Pharaoh ordered all his people to throw every newborn Hebrew boy into the river but let the girls live. This was a cruel attempt to destroy God's people, but God would rescue them.
entries.2:1: A man from the tribe of Levi married a woman from the same tribe. This is simply setting up the family into which Moses would be born.
entries.2:2: The woman became pregnant and had a son, and when she saw he was a fine, healthy child she hid him for three months. She was protecting him because the king had ordered baby boys killed.
entries.2:3: When she could no longer hide him, she made a waterproof basket and set the baby in it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile. She was doing her best to save his life in a desperate situation.
entries.2:4: The baby's older sister stood some distance away to watch and see what would happen to him. She was keeping an eye on her brother out of love and worry.
entries.2:5: The king's daughter came to the river to bathe, saw the basket in the reeds, and sent her servant to bring it to her. This was an unexpected turn that would change the baby's fate.
entries.2:6: When she opened the basket, the baby was crying, and she felt sorry for him and recognized he was one of the Hebrew children. Her compassion moved her to care for a child her father's law had condemned.
entries.2:7: The baby's sister spoke up and offered to find a Hebrew woman to nurse the child for the princess. She was cleverly stepping in to help.
entries.2:8: The princess agreed, and the girl went and brought the baby's own mother. The plan worked out so the mother could care for her son again.
entries.2:9: The princess told the mother to take the child and nurse him, and promised to pay her for it. The mother got her son back and was even paid to raise him.
entries.2:10: When the boy grew older, his mother brought him to the princess, who adopted him as her son and named him Moses, meaning she drew him out of the water. His name would always remind him of how his life was spared.
entries.2:11: When Moses was grown, he went out to see his own people and witnessed how brutally they were forced to work, including an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. He felt a deep connection to the suffering of his people.
entries.2:12: After looking around to make sure no one was watching, Moses killed the Egyptian and buried him in the sand. He took justice into his own hands in secret.
entries.2:13: The next day he went out again and saw two Hebrews fighting, and he asked the one in the wrong why he was fighting his own brother. He tried to stop the conflict among his people.
entries.2:14: The man shot back, asking who made Moses a ruler and judge over them, and whether he planned to kill him too like the Egyptian. Moses realized his secret was out and became afraid.
entries.2:15: When Pharaoh heard what Moses had done, he tried to have him killed, so Moses fled to the land of Midian and sat down by a well. His attempt to help had turned him into a fugitive.
entries.2:16: The priest of Midian had seven daughters who came to the well to draw water for their father's flock. This introduces the family Moses would soon meet.
entries.2:17: Some shepherds came and tried to drive the girls away, but Moses stood up, helped them, and watered their flock for them. He used his strength to defend people being treated unfairly.
entries.2:18: When the daughters returned to their father Reuel, he was surprised they were back so early. He noticed something unusual had happened.
entries.2:19: The daughters explained that an Egyptian had rescued them from the shepherds and even drew water for their flock. They didn't know Moses was a Hebrew, so they described him as an Egyptian.
entries.2:20: Their father asked where the man was and told them to invite him in for a meal. He wanted to show hospitality to the stranger who had helped his daughters.
entries.2:21: Moses agreed to stay and live with the man, who gave him his daughter Zipporah as a wife. Moses found a new home and family in a foreign land.
entries.2:22: Zipporah had a son, and Moses named him Gershom, saying he had been a stranger living in a foreign land. The name reflected his sense of being displaced from his own people.
entries.2:23: After a long time the king of Egypt died, and the Israelites groaned under their hard labor and cried out for help, and their cry reached God. God heard the suffering of his people.
entries.2:24: God heard their groaning and remembered his covenant promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He was faithful to the agreement he had made with their ancestors.
entries.2:25: God looked on the Israelites and showed that he knew their situation and cared about them. He was paying attention to their suffering and was about to act.
entries.3:1: Moses was working as a shepherd for his father-in-law Jethro, a priest in Midian, and he led the flock far out into the desert to Mount Horeb, a mountain associated with God. This shows God can meet people in ordinary, out-of-the-way places while they are doing their daily work.
entries.3:2: Moses saw the angel of the Lord appear in a flame of fire inside a bush; the bush was burning but did not burn up. This was a striking sign that God was present in a way Moses had never seen before.
entries.3:3: Moses decided to walk over and look more closely at this amazing sight, wondering why the bush was not being burned up. Curiosity drew him toward God's unusual sign, and it can draw us closer to God too.
entries.3:4: When the Lord saw Moses coming closer to look, God called him by name from the bush, and Moses answered that he was listening. God notices when we turn toward him and calls us personally.
entries.3:5: God told Moses not to come any closer and to take off his sandals, because the ground he was standing on was holy. God is not casual or ordinary, and the place where he meets us deserves respect.
entries.3:6: God identified himself as the God of Moses' ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and Moses hid his face because he was afraid to look at God. This is the same God who has been faithful to his people for generations, and he is worthy of awe.
entries.3:7: God told Moses that he had seen the suffering of his people in Egypt and had heard their cries because of their harsh masters, and that he knew their sorrows. God is not distant from pain; he sees, hears, and cares about people who are hurting.
entries.3:8: God said he had come down to rescue his people from the Egyptians and bring them out into a good, spacious land that produces plenty. God does not just notice suffering; he acts to rescue people and lead them to something better.
entries.3:9: God repeated that the cry of the Israelites had reached him and that he had seen how cruelly the Egyptians were treating them. God takes the cries of oppressed people seriously and does not ignore what he sees.
entries.3:10: God told Moses that he was sending him to Pharaoh to lead the Israelites out of Egypt. God often uses ordinary people to carry out his rescue plans, even when the task seems far too big.
entries.3:11: Moses asked God who he was to go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt. It is natural to feel unqualified when God asks us to do something hard, but the answer is not in our own ability.
entries.3:12: God promised to be with Moses and gave him a sign: after leading the people out, they would worship God on that same mountain. God's answer to our inadequacy is his presence with us, and he keeps his promises.
entries.3:13: Moses asked what he should tell the Israelites if they asked for the name of the God who sent him. Moses wanted to give the people a clear answer about who this God really is.
entries.3:14: God told Moses to say that I AM has sent him, a name that shows God simply is, always exists, and depends on no one. The God who sends us is the eternal, self-existing God, not a made-up idea.
entries.3:15: God told Moses to call him the Lord, the God of their ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and said this name would be his forever. God wants to be known by name and remembered by every generation as the faithful God of his people.
entries.3:16: God told Moses to gather the elders of Israel and tell them that the Lord, the God of their ancestors, had appeared to him and had taken up their cause because of what was happening to them in Egypt. God wants his people to know he is aware of their trouble and is acting on their behalf.
entries.3:17: God promised to bring the Israelites up out of their misery in Egypt into a land belonging to several other peoples, a land flowing with milk and honey. God's rescue includes a real destination, a good future, not just an escape from the past.
entries.3:18: God said the elders would listen to Moses, and that Moses and the elders should go to Pharaoh and ask permission to travel three days into the desert to offer sacrifice to the Lord their God. God gives his people a clear, respectful request to make, even to a powerful ruler.
entries.3:19: God told Moses plainly that the king of Egypt would not let the people go unless he was forced to. God is honest about opposition, so we should not be surprised when doing his will meets resistance.
entries.3:20: God said he would stretch out his hand and strike Egypt with wonders, and after that Pharaoh would let the people go. God's power, not human persuasion, would finally break the resistance.
entries.3:21: God promised to make the Egyptians favorable toward the Israelites, so that when they left they would not go empty-handed. God can provide for his people even through those who once opposed them.
entries.3:22: God said each Israelite woman should ask her neighbor and any woman living in her house for silver, gold, and clothing, which would be put on their sons and daughters, so the people would take the best of the Egyptians' goods. God was providing for the departing people, and this was understood as fair payment after years of slavery.
entries.4:1: Moses worries that the Israelites won't believe God really sent him. It's natural to fear rejection, but God doesn't dismiss Moses's fear—he answers it.
entries.4:2: God starts with something ordinary that Moses already has in his hand. God often begins with what we already carry rather than something new.
entries.4:3: The staff turns into a snake, and Moses runs in fear. This shows God's power can be startling, not just comforting.
entries.4:4: God tells Moses to grab the snake by the tail, and it turns back into his staff. What frightened Moses becomes an ordinary tool again when he obeys.
entries.4:5: The sign is meant to convince the people that God really appeared to Moses. God gives evidence to help people believe.
entries.4:6: God gives a second sign: Moses's hand becomes diseased and white. It's a visible, physical proof of God's power.
entries.4:7: Moses repeats the action and his hand is healed. God's power works both to harm and to restore.
entries.4:8: God provides a backup sign in case the first one isn't enough. He is patient with people who need more convincing.
entries.4:9: A third sign is given—Nile water turning to blood on dry land. God keeps giving evidence so people have every chance to believe.
entries.4:10: Moses protests that he isn't a good speaker and never has been. He feels inadequate for the job God is giving him.
entries.4:11: God reminds Moses that he made the mouth and controls speech, hearing, and sight. The one who made us is able to help us do what he asks.
entries.4:12: God promises to be with Moses's mouth and teach him what to say. God supplies what he commands.
entries.4:13: Moses asks God to send someone else instead. This is a polite but clear refusal, and it shows how deep his reluctance is.
entries.4:14: God is angry at Moses's continued refusal, yet he still provides help: Aaron, who speaks well, is already on his way. God's anger doesn't cancel his care.
entries.4:15: God will give Moses the words, and Moses will pass them to Aaron to speak. The task is shared, and God is with both of them.
entries.4:16: Aaron will speak to the people for Moses, and Moses will pass on God's words to Aaron. Each has a role in getting God's message across.
entries.4:17: Moses is to carry the staff, which will be used to perform the signs. The ordinary object becomes the tool for God's work.
entries.4:18: Moses asks his father-in-law Jethro for permission to return to Egypt, and Jethro sends him off peacefully. Even a simple family goodbye shows God clearing the way.
entries.4:19: God tells Moses in Midian to go back to Egypt because those who wanted to kill him are dead. The danger that kept him away is gone.
entries.4:20: Moses takes his wife and sons and heads back to Egypt, carrying God's staff. He finally acts on God's command.
entries.4:21: God tells Moses to perform the wonders before Pharaoh but warns that he will harden Pharaoh's heart so he won't let the people go. God's plan includes Pharaoh's resistance.
entries.4:22: God calls Israel his firstborn son. This shows how close and precious the nation is to God.
entries.4:23: God tells Pharaoh to let his son go free to worship, and warns that refusing will cost Pharaoh his own firstborn. The warning is serious and direct.
entries.4:24: On the journey, God confronts Moses and threatens his life. Something in Moses's household was seriously wrong before God.
entries.4:25: Zipporah circumcises her son with a sharp stone and touches Moses's feet with the skin, calling him a husband of blood. She acts to save Moses's life.
entries.4:26: God lets Moses go after this. The circumcision resolved the crisis, and Zipporah's words mark how costly it was.
entries.4:27: God tells Aaron to meet Moses in the wilderness, and Aaron finds him at the mountain of God and greets him warmly. God arranges support and reunion for Moses.
entries.4:28: Moses tells Aaron everything God said and all the signs he was told to do. Sharing God's instructions with a trusted partner prepares them both.
entries.4:29: Moses and Aaron gather all the leaders of Israel. The mission begins with the people's own elders.
entries.4:30: Aaron relays God's words to the people and performs the signs in front of them. The message and the evidence are presented together.
entries.4:31: The people believe, and when they hear God has seen their suffering, they bow in worship. Knowing God cares about their pain moves them to trust and worship.
entries.5:1: Moses and Aaron tell Pharaoh that Israel's God commands him to let the people go into the desert to worship. It shows that God's demand comes before any human ruler's authority.
entries.5:2: Pharaoh says he doesn't know this God and refuses to obey him. It reminds the reader that people in power often dismiss God, but that doesn't make God any less real.
entries.5:3: Moses and Aaron explain they must travel a short distance to worship God, or disaster may fall on them. It shows they are trying to obey God honestly while asking for something reasonable.
entries.5:4: Pharaoh accuses Moses and Aaron of distracting the people from their work and orders them back to labor. It shows how quickly a request for freedom gets twisted into an accusation.
entries.5:5: Pharaoh complains that the Israelites are already numerous and now are being kept from work. It reveals his fear of losing control over a growing people.
entries.5:6: That same day Pharaoh issues orders to the men who supervise the Israelite laborers. It shows that he responds to God's request by making life harder, not easier.
entries.5:7: Pharaoh stops supplying the straw the workers need for making bricks and makes them gather it themselves. It means the people now have to do extra work just to keep the same output.
entries.5:8: Pharaoh demands the same number of bricks while claiming the people are lazy and only want to go worship. It shows him punishing them for a request he refuses to take seriously.
entries.5:9: Pharaoh tells the supervisors to load the men with harder work so they stop listening to Moses. It means he hopes exhaustion will make the people give up on hope.
entries.5:10: The supervisors announce to the people that Pharaoh will no longer provide straw. It marks the moment the new, harsher rules actually reach the workers.
entries.5:11: The people are told to find their own straw wherever they can while keeping production the same. It means the burden falls on them with no help from the government.
entries.5:12: The Israelites scatter across Egypt searching for leftover stalks to use as straw. It shows how the whole people are now consumed with just surviving the day's quota.
entries.5:13: The supervisors keep pushing the workers to meet the same daily output as before. It means the old standard is enforced even though the conditions have gotten worse.
entries.5:14: The Israelite foremen are beaten and asked why they haven't met the quota. It shows that the people caught in the middle get blamed and punished for a system designed to fail.
entries.5:15: The Israelite foremen go to Pharaoh and ask why he is treating his servants this way. It shows them appealing directly to the one person who could change the situation.
entries.5:16: The foremen point out they get no straw, are still told to make bricks, and are beaten for it. It means they are naming the unfairness plainly to Pharaoh himself.
entries.5:17: Pharaoh repeats his charge that they are lazy and only want to go worship the Lord. It shows he refuses to hear their complaint and just repeats his excuse.
entries.5:18: Pharaoh sends them back to work with no straw but the same brick quota. It means the unfair demand stands and there is no relief in sight.
entries.5:19: The foremen realize they are in real trouble because the daily brick quota will not be lowered. It shows them understanding that Pharaoh has no intention of easing their burden.
entries.5:20: The foremen meet Moses and Aaron as they leave Pharaoh's presence. It sets up a confrontation between the people's leaders and God's messengers.
entries.5:21: The foremen blame Moses and Aaron for making Pharaoh hate them and putting them in danger. It shows how quickly hope can turn into anger when things get worse instead of better.
entries.5:22: Moses goes back to God and asks why he has brought trouble on the people and why he was sent at all. It shows that even God's chosen leader can be confused and upset when obedience seems to backfire.
entries.5:23: Moses complains that since he spoke to Pharaoh, things have only gotten worse, and God has not rescued the people. It means Moses is honestly telling God that the situation looks like a failure.
entries.6:1: God tells Moses that he is about to act, and Pharaoh will be forced to let the people go—not just let them leave, but drive them out. It means God is the one who will break Pharaoh's resistance, so Moses can expect God to do what he cannot.
entries.6:2: God introduces himself to Moses by his personal name, Yahweh. It means the God speaking is not a distant force but a specific, personal God who is making himself known.
entries.6:3: God says the patriarchs knew him as the all-powerful God but did not know him by his name Yahweh. It means God is now revealing himself more fully to Moses than he did to earlier generations.
entries.6:4: God reminds Moses that he made a binding agreement with the ancestors to give them the land of Canaan, where they had lived as foreigners. It means God's promise about the land is still standing and he has not forgotten it.
entries.6:5: God says he has heard the groaning of the Israelites under Egyptian slavery and remembers his agreement with their ancestors. It means their suffering has not gone unnoticed, and God is about to act on his promise.
entries.6:6: God tells Moses to tell the Israelites that he will free them from slavery, rescue them from Egyptian power, and redeem them with great acts of judgment. It means God himself is taking responsibility for their rescue, not leaving it to them.
entries.6:7: God promises to make the Israelites his own people and to be their God, and they will know it was he who freed them from Egypt. It means their relationship with God will be based on what he does for them, and they will recognize him through it.
entries.6:8: God promises to bring them into the land he swore to give their ancestors and to give it to them as their own. It means the goal of the rescue is a real place and a real inheritance, guaranteed by God's oath.
entries.6:9: Moses told the people all this, but they did not listen because their spirits were crushed by harsh slavery. It means deep suffering can make it hard to hear good news, and that is not a failure of faith but a real human condition.
entries.6:10: God speaks to Moses again, continuing the conversation. It means God keeps moving his plan forward even when the people are too discouraged to respond.
entries.6:11: God commands Moses to go to Pharaoh and demand that he let the Israelites leave Egypt. It means Moses is being sent back into a hard situation with a clear message from God.
entries.6:12: Moses objects that if his own people won't listen to him, Pharaoh certainly won't, and he mentions his poor speaking ability. It means Moses feels inadequate for the task, and he is honest with God about his fear.
entries.6:13: God gives Moses and Aaron orders concerning both the Israelites and Pharaoh, to bring the people out of Egypt. It means God commissions them directly and keeps them focused on the mission despite the obstacles.
entries.6:14: The text begins a family record, starting with the descendants of Reuben, Israel's firstborn. It means the story now anchors Moses and Aaron in a real family line, showing they belong to the people they are leading.
entries.6:15: The record lists the sons and families of Simeon, Israel's second son. It means the genealogy continues to show the wider family background of the people God is rescuing.
entries.6:16: The record lists Levi's sons and notes that Levi lived to be 137 years old. It means the focus is narrowing toward the family line that will produce Moses and Aaron.
entries.6:17: The record lists Gershon's sons and their family groups. It means the family tree is being traced carefully, generation by generation.
entries.6:18: The record lists Kohath's sons and notes Kohath lived to be 133 years old. It means the line leading to Moses and Aaron is being followed through Kohath.
entries.6:19: The record lists Merari's sons and their family groups among the Levites. It means the Levite family record is being completed before moving to the next generation.
entries.6:20: Amram married Jochebed, his father's sister, and she gave birth to Aaron and Moses; Amram lived to be 137. It means Moses and Aaron are placed directly in the Levite family line, grounding their authority in their ancestry.
entries.6:21: The record lists the sons of Izhar, Kohath's brother. It means the family tree continues to fill in the wider Levite clan.
entries.6:22: The record lists the sons of Uzziel, another of Kohath's sons. It means the genealogy keeps tracing the extended family of the Levites.
entries.6:23: Aaron married Elisheba, and she gave birth to Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. It means Aaron's own family is now recorded, showing the next generation of priests and leaders.
entries.6:24: The record lists the sons of Korah and their family groups. It means the family tree includes the Korahites, who will matter later in Israel's story.
entries.6:25: Eleazar, Aaron's son, married a daughter of Putiel, and she gave birth to Phinehas; the record names the heads of the Levite families. It means the priestly line continues into the next generation.
entries.6:26: The text identifies this same Aaron and Moses as the ones God told to bring the Israelites out of Egypt in organized groups. It means the long family record exists to confirm that these two men are the ones God chose.
entries.6:27: The text says these same men, Moses and Aaron, were the ones who spoke to Pharaoh to let the Israelites go. It means their identity and mission are firmly established before the story continues.
entries.6:28: The text sets the scene: this happened on the day God spoke to Moses in Egypt. It means the narrative is returning to the moment of God's command.
entries.6:29: God tells Moses that he is the Lord and that Moses must tell Pharaoh everything God says to him. It means Moses is to deliver God's message fully, without editing it out of fear.
entries.6:30: Moses again objects that he is a poor speaker and doubts Pharaoh will listen to him. It means Moses is still struggling with fear, and God will have to address his hesitation before the mission moves forward.
entries.7:1: God tells Moses that he will stand before Pharaoh with God's own authority, and Aaron will speak his words for him. It means God equips ordinary people to do a daunting job, so the reader can trust that God supplies what is needed.
entries.7:2: Moses is to pass on exactly what God commands, and Aaron will relay it to Pharaoh, demanding that Israel be freed. The reader learns that faithfulness means speaking God's message clearly rather than editing it.
entries.7:3: God says he will make Pharaoh stubborn, and then multiply miraculous signs in Egypt. This warns the reader that a hard heart can become fixed, while God's wonders still display his power.
entries.7:4: Pharaoh will refuse to listen, so God will act against Egypt with severe judgments and lead his people out. It shows that human resistance cannot stop God's plan to rescue his people.
entries.7:5: When God stretches out his hand against Egypt and rescues Israel, the Egyptians will recognize who the true God is. The reader sees that God's actions are meant to make his identity known, even to those who oppose him.
entries.7:6: Moses and Aaron carried out exactly what God commanded them. Their obedience is a model for the reader of doing what God says, even when it is difficult.
entries.7:7: Moses was eighty and Aaron eighty-three when they delivered God's message to Pharaoh. It reminds the reader that God can call people to important work late in life; age is no barrier.
entries.7:8: God continues speaking to Moses and Aaron, preparing them for the next step. It shows God guiding his servants step by step rather than leaving them on their own.
entries.7:9: If Pharaoh demands a miracle, Aaron is to throw down his staff and it will become a snake. God gives his servants a clear sign to offer, showing he prepares them for the challenges ahead.
entries.7:10: Moses and Aaron did as God said, and Aaron's staff became a snake right in front of Pharaoh and his officials. The reader sees that God's word proves true when it is acted on.
entries.7:11: Pharaoh summoned Egypt's wise men and sorcerers, and they copied the feat with their own techniques. It shows that counterfeit power can imitate God's signs, so the reader should not be fooled by impressive displays alone.
entries.7:12: Each sorcerer's staff became a snake too, but Aaron's staff swallowed theirs. This shows God's power is greater than any rival power, giving the reader confidence in him.
entries.7:13: Even so, Pharaoh remained stubborn and refused to listen, just as God had said. It illustrates how a person can see clear evidence and still harden their heart against God.
entries.7:14: God tells Moses and Aaron that Pharaoh is still stubborn and will not release the people. The reader learns that stubbornness persists even when it costs a person dearly.
entries.7:15: God instructs Moses to meet Pharaoh early in the morning at the riverbank, carrying the staff that became a snake. It shows God's careful timing and preparation, meeting Pharaoh where he is.
entries.7:16: Moses is to tell Pharaoh that the God of the Hebrews demands freedom for his people to worship him, yet Pharaoh has ignored him so far. The reader sees that God's claim on people's lives is stated plainly and persistently.
entries.7:17: God says Pharaoh will learn who the Lord is when Moses strikes the Nile with his staff and turns it to blood. It shows God backs his words with visible proof so that people may know him.
entries.7:18: The fish will die, the river will stink, and Egyptians will be unable to drink from the Nile. The reader sees that rejecting God's command brings real consequences that touch daily life.
entries.7:19: God tells Aaron to stretch out his staff over all Egypt's waters, so that every river, stream, pool, and even water in containers turns to blood. It shows the judgment is total and inescapable, affecting the whole land.
entries.7:20: Moses and Aaron obeyed, and in front of Pharaoh and his officials the Nile's water turned to blood. The reader sees God's warning carried out exactly as promised.
entries.7:21: The fish died, the river stank, and Egyptians could not drink the water, with blood throughout the land. It shows the seriousness of the judgment and how it disrupts ordinary life.
entries.7:22: Egypt's sorcerers copied the feat, and Pharaoh's heart stayed hard so he would not listen, just as God had said. The reader learns that even matching signs do not soften a person determined to resist God.
entries.7:23: Pharaoh simply went home and gave the matter no thought. It shows how someone can dismiss even a dramatic warning, and it challenges the reader not to ignore what God is saying.
entries.7:24: The Egyptians dug around the Nile to find drinking water because they could not use the river. It shows the practical hardship that comes when a leader refuses to heed God.
entries.7:25: A full week passed after God struck the Nile. The reader sees that God's judgments are not fleeting but have lasting weight, giving time for reflection.
entries.8:1: God tells Moses to go to Pharaoh with a simple demand: let the Israelites go so they can worship God. The reader learns that God's first concern is freedom to worship him.
entries.8:2: God warns that refusing will bring frogs all over Egypt. The reader sees that ignoring God's command has real consequences.
entries.8:3: The frogs will be everywhere, even in houses, bedrooms, beds, ovens and bowls. The reader sees that the judgment reaches into everyday, private life, not just public places.
entries.8:4: The frogs will come on Pharaoh, his officials and all his people. The reader sees that no one in power is exempt from the results of refusing God.
entries.8:5: God tells Moses to have Aaron stretch out his staff over the rivers and pools so frogs come up onto the land. The reader sees God using a visible sign through his appointed leader.
entries.8:6: Aaron obeys, and frogs come up and cover the whole land. The reader sees that God's word through Moses and Aaron actually happens.
entries.8:7: Pharaoh's magicians manage to produce frogs too. The reader sees that human power can imitate some things but cannot undo God's work.
entries.8:8: Pharaoh asks Moses and Aaron to pray for the frogs to be removed and promises to let the people go. The reader sees that trouble can make people promise things they later break.
entries.8:9: Moses lets Pharaoh choose the time for the prayer, showing respect and confidence. The reader sees Moses acting with calm authority given by God.
entries.8:10: Pharaoh says tomorrow, and Moses agrees so Pharaoh will know no one is like the Lord. The reader sees that the point of the miracle is to show who God is.
entries.8:11: The frogs will leave Pharaoh, his officials and his people and remain only in the Nile. The reader sees God's judgment being reversed exactly as promised.
entries.8:12: Moses and Aaron leave Pharaoh, and Moses prays about the frogs. The reader sees that prayer is the response to trouble, even trouble God himself sent.
entries.8:13: The Lord answers Moses' prayer and the frogs die off everywhere. The reader sees that God hears and answers prayer.
entries.8:14: The dead frogs are piled up and the land stinks. The reader sees that relief from judgment still leaves a messy reminder behind.
entries.8:15: When the trouble stops, Pharaoh hardens his heart and breaks his promise. The reader sees that people often forget God once things get comfortable again.
entries.8:16: God tells Moses to have Aaron strike the dust so it becomes insects across Egypt. The reader sees God bringing a new judgment through the same leaders.
entries.8:17: Aaron does it, and the dust turns into insects on people and animals everywhere. The reader sees that God's power affects all of creation, not just humans.
entries.8:18: The magicians try to make insects but cannot, even though the insects are on everyone. The reader sees a clear limit to human power compared with God's.
entries.8:19: The magicians tell Pharaoh this is God's doing, but Pharaoh still refuses to listen. The reader sees that even clear evidence can be ignored by a stubborn heart.
entries.8:20: God tells Moses to meet Pharaoh early by the water and repeat the demand to let the people go. The reader sees God giving Pharaoh another chance to obey.
entries.8:21: If Pharaoh refuses, God will send swarms of flies on him, his officials, his people and their houses. The reader sees the warning is specific and serious.
entries.8:22: God will keep the flies out of Goshen where his people live, so Pharaoh will know the Lord is over all the earth. The reader sees God protecting his own people while judging others.
entries.8:23: God will make a clear difference between his people and Pharaoh's people, and the sign will come tomorrow. The reader sees God's timing is set and certain.
entries.8:24: The flies come and fill Pharaoh's house and the whole land, ruining it. The reader sees that God's warning was not empty.
entries.8:25: Pharaoh calls Moses and Aaron and offers a compromise: worship God here in Egypt. The reader sees that partial obedience is often offered instead of full obedience.
entries.8:26: Moses says that would not be right, because the Israelites' sacrifices would offend the Egyptians and could get them killed. The reader sees Moses refusing a plan that would cause real danger and disrespect.
entries.8:27: Moses insists they must travel three days into the desert to worship as God commands. The reader sees that God's instructions are not negotiable.
entries.8:28: Pharaoh agrees to let them go into the desert but not far, and asks Moses to pray for him. The reader sees Pharaoh still trying to control the terms.
entries.8:29: Moses promises to pray for the flies to leave tomorrow and warns Pharaoh not to deceive them again. The reader sees Moses holding Pharaoh accountable while still willing to pray for him.
entries.8:30: Moses leaves Pharaoh and prays to the Lord. The reader sees faithful prayer even after a tense negotiation.
entries.8:31: The Lord answers and removes all the flies, not one left. The reader sees God's complete deliverance in response to prayer.
entries.8:32: But Pharaoh hardens his heart again and does not let the people go. The reader sees that repeated refusal makes a person more set in their ways.
entries.9:1: God tells Moses to go to Pharaoh and demand that he let the Israelites go so they can worship God. It shows God gives Pharaoh a clear chance to obey before judgment comes.
entries.9:2: God warns that if Pharaoh keeps refusing to release the people, there will be consequences. Refusing God's clear command brings trouble, not safety.
entries.9:3: God says a terrible disease will strike Egypt's livestock—horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, sheep, and goats. The things people depend on for work and wealth are not beyond God's reach.
entries.9:4: God will spare the Israelites' animals while Egypt's animals die, showing He makes a clear difference between His people and those who oppose Him. God protects His own even in the middle of judgment.
entries.9:5: God sets an exact time for this to happen: tomorrow. God's warnings are not vague threats; He keeps His word on schedule.
entries.9:6: The next day it happens just as God said—all Egypt's livestock die, but none of Israel's animals are lost. God's word proves completely reliable.
entries.9:7: Pharaoh checks and finds Israel's animals untouched, yet he still refuses to let the people go. Seeing God's protection should soften a heart, but pride can keep someone stubborn.
entries.9:8: God tells Moses and Aaron to take handfuls of soot from a furnace and have Moses throw it into the air in front of Pharaoh. This sets up the next sign in a visible, simple way.
entries.9:9: The dust will spread over Egypt and cause painful boils on people and animals everywhere. God's judgment reaches even the bodies of those who defy Him.
entries.9:10: They do exactly as God said, and boils break out on people and animals all over Egypt. Obeying God's instructions brings about exactly what He promised.
entries.9:11: Egypt's magicians can't even stand before Moses because they are covered in boils too. The powers people trust in fail when God acts.
entries.9:12: God hardens Pharaoh's heart, and he refuses to listen, just as God had said. Persistent refusal of God can lead to a heart that no longer responds.
entries.9:13: God again sends Moses early in the morning to demand that Pharaoh release the people to worship Him. God keeps giving Pharaoh opportunities to obey, even after many refusals.
entries.9:14: This time God will bring the full force of His judgments on Pharaoh, his officials, and his people, so everyone will know no one is like Him. God acts so that people will recognize who He truly is.
entries.9:15: God says He could have wiped Pharaoh and his people off the earth already. The fact that they are still alive is mercy, not weakness.
entries.9:16: God let Pharaoh survive to show His power and make His name known everywhere. Even a stubborn ruler serves God's purpose of displaying who God is.
entries.9:17: God asks Pharaoh why he is still proud and refuses to let the people go. Pride is the root of Pharaoh's stubbornness, and God confronts it directly.
entries.9:18: God announces that tomorrow He will send the worst hailstorm Egypt has ever seen. The warning gives people time to act and shows God's judgment is coming.
entries.9:19: God tells Pharaoh to bring his livestock and workers in from the fields, because anything left outside will be killed by the hail. God's warning is also an invitation to take shelter and be spared.
entries.9:20: Some of Pharaoh's officials fear God's word and quickly bring their servants and animals indoors. Taking God's warnings seriously saves people from harm.
entries.9:21: Those who ignore God's warning leave their servants and animals out in the fields. Disregarding God's word puts people and what they care about in danger.
entries.9:22: God tells Moses to stretch out his hand so hail will fall on all Egypt—on people, animals, and plants. God's judgment covers the whole land, not just part of it.
entries.9:23: Moses raises his staff, and God sends thunder, hail, and fire running along the ground. God's word through Moses brings immediate and powerful results.
entries.9:24: The hail is mixed with fire and is more severe than anything Egypt has seen since it became a nation. This is an unprecedented judgment, showing the seriousness of resisting God.
entries.9:25: The hail strikes everything left in the fields—people, animals, plants, and trees—across Egypt. Nothing exposed is safe when God's judgment falls.
entries.9:26: Only in Goshen, where the Israelites live, is there no hail. God again makes a clear distinction, protecting His people while judging Egypt.
entries.9:27: Pharaoh admits he has sinned and that God is right while he and his people are wrong. Even a hard heart can momentarily acknowledge the truth under pressure.
entries.9:28: Pharaoh begs Moses to pray for the thunder and hail to stop and promises to let the people go. Fear of suffering can produce promises that don't last.
entries.9:29: Moses says he will pray outside the city, and the storm will stop so Pharaoh will know the earth belongs to the Lord. God's power over nature is meant to show He rules over all.
entries.9:30: Moses tells Pharaoh plainly that he and his officials still don't truly fear God. Words of repentance can be empty if the heart hasn't changed.
entries.9:31: The flax and barley were destroyed because the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom. The judgment hits real crops at a real season, causing real loss.
entries.9:32: The wheat and spelt were spared because they grow later and hadn't come up yet. Even in judgment, God's timing leaves some things untouched.
entries.9:33: Moses leaves the city, prays to God, and the thunder, hail, and rain stop. God answers prayer and shows His control over the storm.
entries.9:34: Once the storm stops, Pharaoh sins again and hardens his heart along with his officials. Relief from trouble doesn't automatically change a stubborn heart.
entries.9:35: Pharaoh's heart stays hard and he refuses to let the people go, just as God had said through Moses. God's word proves true even when people refuse to change.
entries.10:1: God tells Moses to go back to Pharaoh, because God himself has made Pharaoh and his officials stubborn. This means God is using Pharaoh's resistance to display his power openly.
entries.10:2: God wants the story of his miracles in Egypt passed down from parents to children and grandchildren. For the reader, it means remembering and telling what God has done keeps faith alive across generations.
entries.10:3: Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh with God's question: how long will you stay proud and refuse to let my people go to worship me? It means pride that resists God only brings trouble.
entries.10:4: God warns that refusing to release the people will bring a plague of locusts the very next day. It shows that ignoring God's warning has real consequences.
entries.10:5: The locusts will be so thick they cover the ground and eat every plant and tree left after the earlier hail. It means the coming judgment will be total, leaving nothing spared.
entries.10:6: The locusts will fill the houses of Pharaoh, his officials, and all Egypt, worse than anything their ancestors ever saw. It means this disaster will be unlike anything in living memory.
entries.10:7: Pharaoh's own officials urge him to let the men go, asking how long he will keep causing ruin and whether he sees Egypt is being destroyed. It means even those around a stubborn leader can see the damage being done.
entries.10:8: Pharaoh calls Moses and Aaron back and agrees to let the people worship, but asks who exactly will go. It shows he is still trying to control the terms rather than fully obey.
entries.10:9: Moses answers that everyone will go—young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds—because they are holding a festival to the Lord. It means wholehearted worship gives God everything, not just a part.
entries.10:10: Pharaoh sarcastically says he will let them and their children go only if the Lord helps them, accusing them of evil intent. It means he is mocking their request and still refusing to truly release them.
entries.10:11: Pharaoh refuses to let the women and children go, allowing only the men, and drives Moses and Aaron out. It means he wants to keep leverage over the people so they must return.
entries.10:12: God tells Moses to stretch out his hand so locusts will come and eat every green plant left in Egypt. It means God is about to carry out the warning he gave.
entries.10:13: Moses raises his staff, and God sends an east wind all day and night that brings the locusts in the morning. It shows God directing even the wind to accomplish his purpose.
entries.10:14: The locusts swarm over the whole land in numbers never seen before or since. It means this plague is unprecedented in its scale.
entries.10:15: The locusts cover the ground until it looks black and eat every green plant and fruit left after the hail. It means nothing green remains anywhere in Egypt.
entries.10:16: Pharaoh quickly calls for Moses and Aaron and admits he has sinned against the Lord and against them. It means even a hard heart can be forced to confess wrongdoing under pressure.
entries.10:17: Pharaoh asks forgiveness just this once and begs Moses to pray that this deadly plague be removed. It means his repentance is shallow and focused only on relief from suffering.
entries.10:18: Moses leaves Pharaoh and prays to the Lord. It shows Moses faithfully interceding even for the one who oppresses his people.
entries.10:19: God sends a strong west wind that carries the locusts into the Red Sea, leaving none in Egypt. It means God completely reverses the disaster in response to prayer.
entries.10:20: But God makes Pharaoh's heart hard again, and he refuses to let the Israelites go. It means relief from judgment does not change a heart that will not truly submit.
entries.10:21: God tells Moses to stretch his hand toward heaven so that darkness falls over Egypt, thick enough that people grope around. It means the next judgment will be a terrifying loss of light.
entries.10:22: Moses stretches out his hand, and deep darkness covers all Egypt for three days. It means the land is plunged into total, unnatural darkness.
entries.10:23: People cannot see each other or leave their places for three days, but the Israelites have light where they live. It means God protects and distinguishes his people even in the middle of judgment.
entries.10:24: Pharaoh calls Moses and offers to let the people worship, but insists their flocks and herds stay behind, with the children allowed to go. It means he is still bargaining and holding back what God requires.
entries.10:25: Moses replies that Pharaoh must also provide animals for burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord. It means worship requires giving God what he asks, not just what is convenient.
entries.10:26: Moses insists all their livestock must go, not one left behind, because they need them for worship and don't yet know what offerings to give. It means complete obedience leaves nothing held back from God.
entries.10:27: But God makes Pharaoh's heart hard, and he refuses to let the people go. It means the cycle of stubbornness continues despite every warning.
entries.10:28: Pharaoh angrily tells Moses to leave and warns that seeing his face again will mean death. It means the relationship between Pharaoh and Moses is now completely broken.
entries.10:29: Moses agrees, saying he will never see Pharaoh's face again. It means the final break has come, and the next encounter will bring the last judgment.
entries.11:1: God tells Moses that one last disaster will hit Egypt, and after it Pharaoh will not just let the Israelites go but will urgently push them out. It means the long struggle is almost over, and God will finish what he started.
entries.11:2: God tells the Israelites to ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold jewelry before they leave. It means God is providing for them as they go, so they won't leave empty-handed.
entries.11:3: God made the Egyptians look kindly on the Israelites, and Moses himself was greatly respected by Pharaoh's officials and the people. It means God can turn people's attitudes around, even in a hostile place.
entries.11:4: Moses announces God's message to Pharaoh: around midnight God himself will pass through Egypt. It means the coming judgment is God's own action, not just a natural event.
entries.11:5: Every firstborn son in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's own heir to the poorest servant girl's child, and the firstborn of the cattle too. It means the judgment reaches every level of society, showing that no one is beyond its reach.
entries.11:6: A huge cry of grief will go up all over Egypt, worse than anything before or after. It means the loss will be felt deeply by the whole nation.
entries.11:7: But among the Israelites, not even a dog will bark at them or their animals. It means God will clearly protect his people and make a visible difference between them and the Egyptians.
entries.11:8: Moses says Pharaoh's own officials will come and beg him to leave with all the people, and then Moses leaves Pharaoh in anger. It means the pressure will finally break, and the exit will happen on God's terms.
entries.11:9: God tells Moses that Pharaoh will refuse to listen, and that is so God's wonders can be multiplied in Egypt. It means the resistance itself becomes part of the larger display of God's power.
entries.11:10: Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, but God hardened Pharaoh's heart and he refused to let Israel go. It means Pharaoh's stubbornness was not overcome by miracles alone, and the story is heading toward the final rescue.
entries.12:1: God speaks to Moses and Aaron while the Israelites are still in Egypt, setting up what comes next. It reminds the reader that God directs his people right where they are.
entries.12:2: God tells them to treat this month as the start of their year, marking a brand-new beginning. For the reader, it shows God can reset the calendar of your life around what he has done.
entries.12:3: Each family is to choose a lamb on the tenth day of the month, one per household. It means every family takes part personally in what God is about to do.
entries.12:4: If a family is too small to eat a whole lamb, they share it with a neighbor, based on how many people there are. It teaches that God's provision is shared, and no one needs to be left out.
entries.12:5: The lamb must be healthy and unblemished, a one-year-old male, from the sheep or goats. The point is that God deserves the best, not leftovers.
entries.12:6: They keep the lamb until the fourteenth day, then the whole community kills it at twilight. It shows this is a shared act of obedience at a set time, not a private whim.
entries.12:7: They put some of the lamb's blood on the doorframe of the house where they eat. The blood marks the home as belonging to God and under his protection.
entries.12:8: That night they eat the roasted lamb with flatbread and bitter herbs. The bitter herbs likely recall the bitterness of slavery, so the meal holds both rescue and hardship.
entries.12:9: The lamb must be roasted whole over fire, not eaten raw or boiled. It's a simple, complete offering, done exactly as God says.
entries.12:10: Nothing is to be left until morning; leftovers are burned. It teaches trust that God provides fresh each day rather than hoarding.
entries.12:11: They eat ready to travel, with shoes on and staff in hand, and they eat quickly. It means being ready to move the moment God acts.
entries.12:12: God himself will pass through Egypt that night, striking the firstborn of people and animals and judging Egypt's gods. It shows God is the one who rescues, and he confronts every rival power.
entries.12:13: The blood on the houses is a sign; when God sees it, he passes over that home and no harm comes. For the reader, it pictures being shielded by a mark God himself recognizes.
entries.12:14: This day is to be remembered and celebrated as a feast to the Lord for all generations. It means God's rescue is worth remembering and passing on, not forgetting.
entries.12:15: For seven days they eat only flatbread, and anyone who eats leavened bread is cut off from the community. It calls for wholehearted obedience and marks this time as set apart.
entries.12:16: The first and seventh days are holy gatherings with no work except preparing food. Rest and worship are built into the celebration, not squeezed around busyness.
entries.12:17: They keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread because on this day God brought them out of Egypt. The feast is tied to real rescue, and it's to be kept for all generations.
entries.12:18: From the evening of the fourteenth day to the evening of the twenty-first, they eat flatbread. It sets a clear, memorable rhythm for the whole week.
entries.12:19: No leaven may be in their houses for seven days, and anyone who eats leavened bread is cut off, whether foreigner or native. It shows that belonging to God's people means sharing the same commitment.
entries.12:20: They are to eat nothing with leaven anywhere they live. It's a simple, everyday rule that keeps the memory of rescue present in ordinary meals.
entries.12:21: Moses tells Israel's leaders to pick out lambs for their families and kill the Passover lamb. It moves the instructions from God to the people's actual hands.
entries.12:22: They dip a bunch of hyssop in the blood and mark the doorframe, and no one leaves the house until morning. It means staying put under God's protection and trusting his word for safety.
entries.12:23: When God passes through to strike Egypt, he will see the blood and pass over that door, not letting death enter. It shows God's protection is based on the sign he told them to make, not on their worthiness.
entries.12:24: They are to keep this practice as a permanent order for themselves and their children. It means faith is meant to be handed down, not kept private.
entries.12:25: When they reach the land God promised, they are to keep this act of worship. It means remembering God's rescue continues even after life gets settled and comfortable.
entries.12:26: Children will ask what this ceremony means. It assumes questions are welcome and that faith is explained, not just performed.
entries.12:27: They answer that it is the Lord's Passover, when he passed over Israel's homes and kept their families safe. The people bow in worship, showing that remembering God's rescue leads to gratitude.
entries.12:28: The Israelites went and did exactly as the Lord commanded through Moses and Aaron. It shows obedience in action, not just agreement in words.
entries.12:29: At midnight the Lord struck every firstborn in Egypt, from Pharaoh's heir to the prisoner's, and the firstborn of cattle too. It's the decisive act of judgment that breaks Egypt's hold.
entries.12:30: Pharaoh and all Egypt wake to a great cry, because there is no house without someone dead. It shows the terrible cost of refusing God, felt across the whole land.
entries.12:31: Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron at night and tells them to leave with the Israelites and worship the Lord. The very ruler who resisted now urges them out.
entries.12:32: Pharaoh tells them to take their flocks and herds and go, and asks for a blessing. Even in defeat he asks God's people to bless him.
entries.12:33: The Egyptians urge the Israelites to leave quickly, saying they will all die otherwise. Fear drives them to push God's people out.
entries.12:34: The people take their bread dough before it rises, carrying it in basins on their shoulders. It shows how sudden the departure was, leaving no time for normal preparations.
entries.12:35: The Israelites do as Moses said and ask the Egyptians for silver, gold, and clothing. They leave not empty-handed but with what was freely given.
entries.12:36: The Lord made the Egyptians favorable toward them, so they gave what was asked and the Israelites carried off Egypt's wealth. God provides for his people even through their former oppressors.
entries.12:37: The Israelites travel from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, plus children. It shows the scale of the rescue: a whole people on the move.
entries.12:38: A mixed group of other people goes with them, along with large flocks and herds. God's rescue draws in others and includes their animals too.
entries.12:39: They bake flatbread from the dough they brought, because they were sent out so fast there was no time for yeast. The unleavened bread is a lasting reminder of a hurried escape.
entries.12:40: The Israelites had lived in Egypt for four hundred and thirty years. It highlights how long they waited, and that God's promise held through generations.
entries.12:41: God kept his promise exactly on time—after 430 years, the people left Egypt on the very day he had planned. It reminds us that God's timing is precise, even when the wait feels long.
entries.12:42: This night was set aside to remember how God rescued his people from Egypt. God's people are to keep remembering his rescue through every generation.
entries.12:43: God told Moses and Aaron that the Passover meal was only for his own people, not for outsiders. Belonging to God's family was required to share in this meal.
entries.12:44: A servant bought with money could join the meal once he was circumcised. So even a servant could belong fully to God's people and share in the Passover.
entries.12:45: A foreign visitor or a hired worker could not eat the Passover meal. Sharing in it required being part of God's people, not just passing through.
entries.12:46: The whole lamb had to be eaten in one house, with nothing carried outside and no bone broken. The meal was to be kept whole and complete, just as God commanded.
entries.12:47: The whole community of Israel was to celebrate this feast together. It was a shared observance for all of God's people, not a private ritual.
entries.12:48: A foreigner living among them could join the Passover if all the males in his family were circumcised, making him like a native-born Israelite. God's people were open to outsiders who fully committed to him.
entries.12:49: The same rule applied to native-born Israelites and to foreigners living among them. God's law treated both groups equally.
entries.12:50: The Israelites did exactly what God commanded through Moses and Aaron. Obedience to God's instructions was the right response to his rescue.
entries.12:51: On that very day, God brought the Israelites out of Egypt in organized groups. God acted decisively to free his people, just as he had promised.
entries.13:1: God speaks directly to Moses here, setting up the instructions that follow. It shows that what comes next is God's own command, not Moses' idea.
entries.13:2: Every firstborn male, whether a child or an animal, belongs to God because he spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt. The reader is meant to see that God has a claim on the first and best of what people have.
entries.13:3: Moses tells the people to remember this day forever as the day God freed them from slavery in Egypt. For the reader, it means freedom from bondage is something worth remembering and celebrating, not forgetting.
entries.13:4: This pins the event to a specific time, the month of Abib, so the memory stays tied to a real date. It reminds the reader that God's rescue happened in actual history, not in a story.
entries.13:5: Once God brings them into the land he promised, they are to keep this practice there. It teaches the reader that remembering God's rescue should shape how you live once you've received what he promised.
entries.13:6: For a week they eat only flatbread, and the last day is a feast to God. The reader sees that remembrance involves both restraint and celebration.
entries.13:7: No leaven at all is to be found anywhere among them for the whole week. It shows the reader that this memory is meant to fill their whole life, not just one corner of it.
entries.13:8: Parents are to explain to their children that this practice is about what God did for them personally. It tells the reader that faith is passed on by telling the next generation what God has done.
entries.13:9: This practice is like a visible reminder worn close, keeping God's law on their lips. For the reader, it means God's rescue should stay constantly in mind and in conversation.
entries.13:10: The command is to keep this observance every year at the set time. It teaches the reader that remembering God's goodness is a regular habit, not a one-time event.
entries.13:11: God will keep his promise and bring them into the land. The reader is reminded that God's commands come with his promises, and he does what he said.
entries.13:12: Every firstborn male, of people and animals, is to be set apart for God. It shows the reader that God deserves the first and best, since he spared his people.
entries.13:13: A donkey's firstborn can be bought back with a lamb, but firstborn sons must always be bought back. The reader sees that redemption costs something, and that human life is treated with special care.
entries.13:14: When a child asks why they do this, the parent tells the story of God's rescue from Egypt. It teaches the reader to be ready to explain their faith simply when asked.
entries.13:15: Because Pharaoh refused to let Israel go, God struck down Egypt's firstborn, so Israel's firstborn are now dedicated to God or bought back. The reader sees that this practice looks back to God's judgment on Egypt and his mercy on Israel.
entries.13:16: Again this is a reminder worn close, because God brought them out by his strong hand. For the reader, it means God's rescue should be remembered constantly, like something you can't miss.
entries.13:17: God avoided the short route through Philistine land because he knew war might scare the people into going back to Egypt. It shows the reader that God knows our weaknesses and leads us in ways we can handle.
entries.13:18: Instead God led them the long way around, through the desert near the Red Sea, and they marched out ready for battle. The reader learns that God's longer path can still be the right one.
entries.13:19: Moses carried Joseph's bones along, keeping the promise made long ago that God would bring Israel back. It shows the reader that keeping old promises and trusting God's future word matters.
entries.13:20: They travel from Succoth and camp at Etham, on the edge of the desert. It's a simple record of the journey, reminding the reader that following God is a step-by-step process.
entries.13:21: God himself led them, a cloud by day and a fire by night, so they could travel at any hour. The reader is shown that God guides his people personally and never leaves them in the dark.
entries.13:22: The cloud and fire stayed with them constantly, day and night. It reassures the reader that God's presence and guidance are continuous, not occasional.
entries.14:1: God speaks directly to Moses, showing that he is guiding his people step by step. For the reader, it means God still takes the lead in the lives of those who follow him.
entries.14:2: God tells the Israelites to turn back and camp in a specific spot by the sea, which seems like an odd move. For the reader, it shows that God's directions don't always make sense at the time but are part of a bigger plan.
entries.14:3: God predicts that Pharaoh will think the Israelites are lost and trapped in the desert. For the reader, it means God knows in advance what enemies will think and do.
entries.14:4: God will use Pharaoh's stubbornness to show his own power, and the Egyptians will come to know who God is. For the reader, it means God can turn even hard hearts into a display of his greatness.
entries.14:5: When Pharaoh hears the people have fled, he and his officials regret letting them go because they lost their workforce. For the reader, it shows how quickly people change their minds when they lose something they value.
entries.14:6: Pharaoh gets his chariot ready and gathers his people for pursuit. For the reader, it shows how fast a powerful person can move against those God is protecting.
entries.14:7: Pharaoh takes six hundred of Egypt's best chariots along with their officers. For the reader, it shows the overwhelming force that was coming against a defenseless people.
entries.14:8: God confirms Pharaoh's hard heart, and Pharaoh chases the Israelites, who had left boldly. For the reader, it shows that God's people can move forward with courage even when danger follows.
entries.14:9: The Egyptian army catches up to the Israelites camped by the sea. For the reader, it shows that trouble can close in fast, even when you're following God's directions.
entries.14:10: The Israelites see the Egyptian army approaching and are terrified, so they cry out to God. For the reader, it's natural to feel fear when danger appears, and crying out to God is the right response.
entries.14:11: The Israelites panic and blame Moses, sarcastically asking if there weren't enough graves in Egypt. For the reader, it shows how fear can make people lash out at their leaders.
entries.14:12: The people remind Moses they had said it was better to stay as slaves in Egypt than die in the desert. For the reader, it shows how quickly people prefer familiar hardship over uncertain freedom.
entries.14:13: Moses tells the people to stand still and not be afraid, promising they will see God rescue them and never see these Egyptians again. For the reader, it means God's rescue is something you watch for, not something you have to engineer yourself.
entries.14:14: You do not have to fight this battle alone. God will handle what you cannot; your part is to stay calm and let him work.
entries.14:15: God tells Moses to stop praying and start moving the people forward. For the reader, it means there's a time to pray and a time to act on what God has already said.
entries.14:16: God tells Moses to raise his staff and stretch out his hand over the sea so it will split and the people can walk through on dry ground. For the reader, it shows God using a simple, obedient action to do something impossible.
entries.14:17: God will harden the Egyptians' hearts so they follow Israel into the sea, and God will gain honor over Pharaoh's army. For the reader, it means God's glory will be seen even in the defeat of those who oppose him.
entries.14:18: The Egyptians will recognize that the Lord is God when he defeats Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen. For the reader, it means God's power will eventually be obvious even to those who don't believe.
entries.14:19: The angel of God and the pillar of cloud move from in front of Israel to behind them. For the reader, it shows God positioning himself as a shield between his people and their enemies.
entries.14:20: The cloud comes between the two armies, bringing darkness to one side while the Israelites travel through the night, and the armies never meet. For the reader, it means God can separate and protect his people from danger in ways they can't see.
entries.14:21: Moses stretches out his hand, and God sends a strong east wind all night that parts the sea and turns it into dry ground. For the reader, it shows God using natural forces over time to accomplish a miracle.
entries.14:22: The Israelites walk through the sea on dry ground with walls of water on both sides. For the reader, it means God can make a safe path right through what looks like certain death.
entries.14:23: The Egyptians chase the Israelites right into the middle of the sea with all their horses and chariots. For the reader, it shows how blind pursuit of God's people can lead someone into their own trap.
entries.14:24: During the last watch of the night, God looks down from the pillar of fire and cloud and throws the Egyptian army into confusion. For the reader, it means God acts at just the right moment to disrupt the plans of those who pursue his people.
entries.14:25: God jams the chariot wheels so they're hard to drive, and the Egyptians realize the Lord is fighting for Israel and decide to flee. For the reader, it shows that even enemies can recognize when God is on someone's side.
entries.14:26: God tells Moses to stretch out his hand over the sea so the waters will come back on the Egyptians and their chariots. For the reader, it means the same water that saved Israel will judge their enemies.
entries.14:27: At dawn, as Moses stretches out his hand, the sea flows back and meets the fleeing Egyptians, and God destroys them in the middle of the sea. For the reader, it shows that God's rescue of his people and his judgment on their enemies happen together.
entries.14:28: The waters cover the chariots, horsemen, and the whole Egyptian army that chased Israel into the sea, and not one survives. For the reader, it means God's deliverance is complete and leaves no threat behind.
entries.14:29: The Israelites walk through the sea on dry ground with walls of water on both sides. For the reader, it repeats the miracle to show that God's people pass through safely while their enemies don't.
entries.14:30: That day God saves Israel from the Egyptians, and Israel sees their enemies dead on the shore. For the reader, it means God's rescue is real and visible, not just a feeling.
entries.14:31: Israel sees the great thing God did to the Egyptians, and the people fear the Lord and put their trust in him and in Moses. For the reader, it shows that seeing God's faithfulness builds trust and respect for him and for the leaders he uses.
entries.15:1: This is a victory song Moses and the Israelites sang after God rescued them from Egypt's army. It invites the reader to thank God when he brings you through a hard situation.
entries.15:2: God himself is the source of strength, help, and rescue for his people. The reader can trust God personally and praise him, not just as a distant idea but as their own God.
entries.15:3: God is described as a powerful warrior who fights for his people. It means God is not passive when his people are in danger; he acts on their behalf.
entries.15:4: God threw Egypt's chariots, army, and best officers into the sea. It shows that even the strongest human power cannot stand against God when he defends his people.
entries.15:5: The Egyptian army sank and disappeared under the water like a stone. The reader sees that God's rescue was complete and final.
entries.15:6: God's great power broke down those who opposed him. It reminds the reader that God's strength is real and able to overcome any enemy.
entries.15:7: When God rises in power, those who fight against him are crushed and burned up quickly. It warns the reader that opposing God is futile.
entries.15:8: God's breath piled the waters up like a wall so the Israelites could pass through. It shows God controlling nature itself to save his people.
entries.15:9: Egypt boasted that it would chase, catch, and plunder the Israelites. It shows how quickly human pride and cruelty can be stopped by God.
entries.15:10: God sent the wind and the sea covered the Egyptians, who sank like lead. The same waters that saved Israel destroyed their enemies.
entries.15:11: No other god compares to the Lord, who is holy, awesome, and does wonders. The reader is invited to hold God in awe as unique and worthy of praise.
entries.15:12: God's power opened the earth to swallow his enemies. It pictures complete defeat for those who set themselves against him.
entries.15:13: God led his people forward with mercy and strength toward his holy place. The reader can trust that God guides those he has claimed as his own.
entries.15:14: News of God's power made other nations tremble with fear. It shows that God's reputation goes ahead of his people and protects them.
entries.15:15: The leaders of Edom, Moab, and Canaan were terrified and lost their courage. It means no surrounding nation could stop what God was doing.
entries.15:16: Fear froze the other peoples until God's people had safely passed by. God's strong arm held back every threat during the journey.
entries.15:17: God will bring his people in and plant them securely in the land that belongs to him, where his dwelling is. It points to lasting safety and a home with God.
entries.15:18: The Lord rules as King forever and ever. The reader can rest in the fact that God's reign never ends or weakens.
entries.15:19: This verse sums up the story: Pharaoh's horses and chariots were drowned, but Israel walked through the sea on dry ground. It is a clear picture of God saving one group and judging the other.
entries.15:20: Miriam, Aaron's sister and a prophet, led the women in music and dancing. It shows that celebration and leadership in worship were shared by women too.
entries.15:21: Miriam sang the same victory song back to the people. It invites everyone, not just leaders, to join in praising God for his rescue.
entries.15:22: Moses led Israel away from the sea into a desert where they found no water for three days. It shows that even after a great rescue, hard times still come.
entries.15:23: They reached a place called Marah, but the water there was too bitter to drink. The reader sees that real need and disappointment can follow right after a spiritual high point.
entries.15:24: The people complained to Moses, asking what they would drink. It shows how quickly fear and thirst can turn gratitude into grumbling.
entries.15:25: God answered Moses' prayer by showing him a tree that made the water drinkable. Here God also gave the people a rule and tested their trust in him.
entries.15:26: God promised that if the people listened to him and obeyed, he would keep them from the diseases he had brought on Egypt. He calls himself their healer, so the reader sees that obedience and trust bring life.
entries.15:27: They came to Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees, and they camped by the water. After the bitter water, God provided a place of rest and plenty.
entries.16:1: The Israelites left Elim and traveled into the desert of Sin about a month and a half after leaving Egypt. It marks the start of a hard season in a barren place, where their trust in God would be tested.
entries.16:2: The whole community complained against Moses and Aaron in the desert. When people are scared and hungry, they often blame their leaders instead of bringing their fears to God.
entries.16:3: The people said they would rather have died in Egypt, where they had plenty of food, than be brought out to starve in the desert. It shows how quickly hard times can make us romanticize the past and forget what God has already done.
entries.16:4: God told Moses he would rain down bread from heaven, and the people were to gather just enough each day. God was testing whether they would trust him and follow his instructions day by day.
entries.16:5: On the sixth day they were to gather twice as much and prepare it in advance. God was already building a rhythm of rest into their lives before he gave the formal Sabbath command.
entries.16:6: Moses and Aaron told the people that by evening they would know it was the Lord who brought them out of Egypt. God was about to answer their complaint in a way that showed his hand, not Moses'.
entries.16:7: They would see God's glory in the morning, because he had heard their grumbling. Moses reminded them that their complaints were really aimed at God, not at him and Aaron.
entries.16:8: Moses said God would give them meat in the evening and bread in the morning, because he had heard their outcry. Their grumbling was not against human leaders but against the Lord himself.
entries.16:9: Moses told Aaron to gather all the people before the Lord because he had heard their complaining. God was inviting the whole community to come near and see what he would do.
entries.16:10: While Aaron was speaking, the people looked toward the desert and saw the glory of the Lord appear in the cloud. God showed up visibly right in the middle of their grumbling.
entries.16:11: The Lord spoke to Moses. This short line sets up God's direct answer to the people's complaint.
entries.16:12: God said he had heard the Israelites' complaints and would give them meat at night and bread in the morning. The point was that they would know he is the Lord their God, not just that their stomachs would be filled.
entries.16:13: That evening quail came and covered the camp, and in the morning there was dew around the tents. God kept his promise exactly as he said he would.
entries.16:14: When the dew dried, a small round substance like frost was left on the ground. Something ordinary-looking appeared, but it was God's provision.
entries.16:15: The Israelites asked each other what it was, because they had no idea, and Moses told them it was the bread the Lord had given them. God's provision can show up in ways we don't recognize at first.
entries.16:16: God told each person to gather only as much as they needed, about one omer per person, according to family size. The rule was designed to teach them to trust God for daily needs rather than hoard.
entries.16:17: The people did as they were told, though some gathered more and some less. It shows that people respond to God's instructions in different ways, even when the command is clear.
entries.16:18: When they measured it, the one who gathered much had nothing left over and the one who gathered little had enough. God made sure everyone's need was met, regardless of how much they collected.
entries.16:19: Moses told them not to keep any of it until morning. This was a direct test of whether they would trust God to provide again the next day.
entries.16:20: Some people ignored Moses and kept some until morning, and it bred worms and stank, which made Moses angry. Hoarding what God provides out of fear ends up spoiling the very gift.
entries.16:21: They gathered it every morning, each as much as they needed, and by the time the sun was hot it melted away. God's provision came fresh each day and could not be stockpiled.
