entries.30:32: The oil was not to be poured on ordinary people, and no one was to make a similar blend. What is holy to God must be kept holy.
entries.30:33: Anyone who made a copy of the oil or put it on a non-priest would be cut off from the people. Misusing holy things had serious consequences.
entries.30:34: God told Moses to take equal amounts of sweet spices—stacte, onycha, galbanum—along with pure frankincense. The incense was made from carefully chosen ingredients.
entries.30:35: These were to be blended by a perfumer, mixed with salt, to make a pure and holy incense. Salt likely signified purity and lasting quality.
entries.30:36: Some of the incense was to be crushed to powder and placed in front of the ark in the Tent of Meeting, where God met with Moses, and it was most holy. It was reserved for the place of God's presence.
entries.30:37: The people were not to make this incense for their own personal use; it was to be kept holy to the Lord. What belonged to God was not for ordinary enjoyment.
entries.30:38: Anyone who made a similar incense just to enjoy its sweet smell would be cut off from the people. Treating holy things as common had serious consequences.
entries.31:1: God begins speaking to Moses again on the mountain. This reminds the reader that what follows comes directly from God.
entries.31:2: God chose a specific man, Bezalel, by name for a special job. It shows God picks ordinary people for His work and knows them personally.
entries.31:3: God filled Bezalel with His Spirit and gave him skill, understanding, and know-how for craftwork. The reader can see that practical talents are gifts from God.
entries.31:4: Bezalel was given ability to make beautiful things out of gold, silver, and bronze. This shows God cares about careful, skilled work done for Him.
entries.31:5: He could also cut and set stones and work with wood in every kind of craft. God gives people many different practical skills to serve His purposes.
entries.31:6: God chose Oholiab to work alongside Bezalel and gave skill to everyone else who was able. God works through teams, and He supplies the ability they need.
entries.31:7: The work included the meeting tent, the ark of the law, and its cover, plus everything for the tent. These were the central items where God would meet with His people.
entries.31:8: They were also to make the table and its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, and the altar for burning incense. Each item had a set purpose in worship.
entries.31:9: The list continues with the altar for burnt offerings, its utensils, and the basin with its stand. Even the practical washing items were part of the holy setup.
entries.31:10: They were to make the woven garments, including the holy clothes for Aaron and his sons to wear as priests. These clothes marked them out for their special role serving God.
entries.31:11: They were also to prepare the holy oil and the sweet-smelling incense for the holy place. Everything was to be done exactly as God commanded.
entries.31:12: God speaks to Moses again. This marks a new instruction that follows the building plans.
entries.31:13: God tells Israel to keep His Sabbaths as a lasting sign that He is the one who makes them holy. For the reader, rest is a visible reminder that God sets His people apart.
entries.31:14: The Sabbath was to be treated as holy, and breaking it carried the severe penalty of being cut off from the people. This shows how seriously God took this sign of belonging to Him.
entries.31:15: Work was allowed for six days, but the seventh was a day of complete rest holy to God, and working on it was punishable by death. The reader sees that God built rest into life and expected it to be honored.
entries.31:16: Israel was to keep the Sabbath through every generation as a permanent agreement. It was meant to be a lasting practice, not a one-time rule.
entries.31:17: The Sabbath was a permanent sign between God and Israel, rooted in God resting after creating the world. It reminds the reader that rest and delight are part of God's own pattern.
entries.31:18: When God finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, He gave him two stone tablets written by God Himself. This shows the law came from God directly, not from human opinion.
entries.32:1: The people got impatient waiting for Moses to come back down the mountain, so they asked Aaron to make them a visible god to lead them. It shows how quickly we can turn away from God when we feel abandoned or things take too long.
entries.32:2: Aaron told the people to hand over the gold earrings from their families. He was going along with their wrong request instead of standing up for what was right.
entries.32:3: Everyone gave their gold earrings to Aaron without objection. The whole community joined in this wrong action together.
entries.32:4: Aaron melted the gold and shaped it into a calf statue, and the people declared it to be the god who brought them out of Egypt. They replaced the real God with something they had made themselves.
entries.32:5: Aaron built an altar in front of the calf and announced a festival to the Lord. He tried to mix worship of the real God with the idol they had just made.
entries.32:6: The people got up early to offer sacrifices and then sat down to eat and party wildly. Their worship turned into self-indulgence rather than honoring God.
entries.32:7: God told Moses to go down quickly because the people had corrupted themselves. God saw exactly what was happening and called it evil.
entries.32:8: God described how the people had already turned from his commands and were worshiping the metal calf. They had broken their promise to follow God alone.
entries.32:9: God told Moses that these people were stubborn and refused to change their ways. Stubbornness against God is a serious problem he sees clearly.
entries.32:10: God told Moses to step aside because his anger was burning and he wanted to destroy the people, then start over with Moses. God's anger against sin is real and serious.
entries.32:11: Moses pleaded with God, asking why his anger was burning against the people he had rescued with such power. Moses stood up for the people instead of accepting the offer to replace them.
entries.32:12: Moses worried that the Egyptians would say God brought his people out only to kill them in the mountains. He asked God to turn from his anger and not bring disaster.
entries.32:13: Moses reminded God of his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel to make their descendants as numerous as the stars and give them the land forever. He appealed to God's own faithfulness.
entries.32:14: So the Lord changed his mind and did not carry out the punishment he had threatened. God listened to Moses's prayer and showed mercy.
entries.32:15: Moses came down the mountain carrying the two stone tablets of the law, written on both sides. He was bringing God's commands to a people who had already broken them.
entries.32:16: The tablets were made by God himself, and the writing on them was God's own writing carved into the stone. These were not human documents but directly from God.
entries.32:17: Joshua heard the loud noise from the camp and thought it sounded like a battle. He misread what was happening because he only heard the sound.
entries.32:18: Moses told Joshua it wasn't the sound of victory or defeat in war, but the sound of singing. The noise was from their wild party, not a battle.
entries.32:19: When Moses got close enough to see the calf statue and the people dancing, he was furious and smashed the stone tablets at the foot of the mountain. His anger showed how seriously the people had broken God's law.
entries.32:20: Moses burned the calf, crushed it to powder, scattered it in water, and made the Israelites drink it. He destroyed the idol completely and made them face what they had done.
entries.32:21: Moses asked Aaron what the people had done to him that led him to bring such a great sin on them. He held Aaron responsible for letting this happen.
entries.32:22: Aaron asked Moses not to be angry and said the people were prone to evil. He tried to excuse himself by blaming the people's bad tendencies.
entries.32:23: Aaron recounted that the people had asked him to make them a god because they didn't know what had happened to Moses. He described the request but avoided taking responsibility.
entries.32:24: Aaron claimed he simply told them to hand over their gold, threw it into the fire, and out came this calf. He made it sound like it happened by accident, dodging his own role.
entries.32:25: Moses saw that the people were out of control and that Aaron had let them run wild, making them a disgrace before their enemies. Bad leadership had left the people shameful and chaotic.
entries.32:26: Moses stood at the entrance to the camp and called for anyone on the Lord's side to come to him, and the Levites gathered to him. He gave people a clear choice about where they stood.
entries.32:27: Moses told the Levites that God commanded each man to take his sword and go through the camp, killing even close relatives. This was a severe judgment on the people's rebellion.
entries.32:28: The Levites did what Moses said, and about three thousand people died that day. The consequences of the idolatry were deadly and serious.
entries.32:29: Moses told the Levites they had set themselves apart for the Lord that day, even at the cost of their own sons and brothers, and that blessing was on them. Their loyalty to God had come before family ties.
entries.32:30: The next day Moses told the people their sin was great, and he would go up to the Lord to see if he could get forgiveness for them. Moses acted as a mediator, seeking mercy for a guilty people.
entries.32:31: Moses went back to the Lord and admitted that the people had committed a great sin by making a gold god. He was honest about the seriousness of what they had done.
entries.32:32: Moses asked God to forgive them, and if not, to remove his own name from God's book. He was willing to give up his own place rather than see the people rejected.
entries.32:33: The Lord told Moses that whoever had sinned against him would be removed from his book. Each person is accountable to God for their own wrongdoing.
entries.32:34: God told Moses to lead the people on to the place he had promised, with his angel going ahead, but he would still punish them for their sin at the right time. Forgiveness did not erase all consequences.
entries.32:35: The Lord struck the people with punishment because they had worshiped the calf Aaron made. Their idolatry brought real consequences on the community.
entries.33:1: God tells Moses to lead the people out of Egypt toward the land he promised long ago to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and their descendants. It means God still keeps his old promises even after the people have done wrong.
entries.33:2: God promises to send an angel ahead of them to drive out the peoples already living in the land. The reader can see that God clears the way, but this verse alone doesn't mean he will be close to them.
entries.33:3: God will bring them to a rich, good land, but he says he will not travel among them because they are stubborn and he might destroy them on the way. It shows that sin puts distance between people and God, even when his gifts continue.
entries.33:4: When the people heard this bad news they mourned and stopped wearing their jewelry. It shows real sorrow over losing God's nearness, not just over losing a gift.
entries.33:5: God calls them stubborn and says that if he came among them even briefly he might destroy them, so they should remove their ornaments while he decides what to do. It means God takes their hard hearts seriously and calls for humility.
entries.33:6: So the Israelites stripped off their ornaments at Mount Horeb and did not wear them again. It marks a lasting change of attitude, showing they were willing to give up something precious to show sorrow.
entries.33:7: Moses set up the meeting tent outside the camp, away from the people, and anyone who wanted to pray to the Lord went out there. It means seeking God now required going outside the camp, a sign that fellowship with him had been disrupted.
entries.33:8: Whenever Moses walked out to the tent, everyone stood at their tent doors and watched him until he went inside. It shows the people's respect for Moses and their attention to anyone who meets with God.
entries.33:9: When Moses entered the tent, the cloud came down and stood at the entrance while the Lord spoke with him. It means God really was present and speaking, and the cloud was a visible sign of that.
entries.33:10: All the people saw the cloud at the tent door and bowed down with their faces to the ground, each at his own tent. It shows that when God's presence was visible, the people responded with worship.
entries.33:11: The Lord spoke with Moses face to face, like friends talking, and Joshua stayed behind in the tent. It means Moses had an unusually close relationship with God, and Joshua was being prepared to lead.
entries.33:12: Moses reminds God that he was told to lead the people but not told who would go with him, and he recalls God's promise of favor and personal knowledge of him. It shows Moses praying honestly and holding God to his own words.
entries.33:13: Moses asks to know God's ways so he can truly know him and be sure of his favor, and he asks God to remember that this nation is his own people. It means Moses wants more than guidance; he wants a deeper relationship with God.
entries.33:14: God answers that he himself will go with Moses and give him rest. It means God grants the nearness Moses asked for and promises relief from the burden of the journey.
entries.33:15: Moses says that if God himself will not go with them, they should not leave that place at all. It shows that God's presence mattered more to Moses than reaching the destination.
entries.33:16: Moses argues that God's going with them is exactly what marks Israel as different from every other people. It means God's presence, not their own strength, is what makes his people distinct.
entries.33:17: The Lord agrees to do what Moses asks because Moses has found favor with him and God knows him by name. It shows that God listens to prayer and values a close relationship with a person.
entries.33:18: Moses asks to see God's glory. It is a bold request to experience God's greatness and goodness more directly.
entries.33:19: God says he will show his goodness and proclaim his name before Moses, and he will be kind and merciful to whomever he chooses. It means God reveals himself freely, and mercy is his choice to give, not something anyone earns.
entries.33:20: God says Moses cannot see his face, because no one can see God fully and survive. It means God is far greater and more holy than humans can handle directly.
entries.33:21: God tells Moses there is a place near him where Moses can stand on a rock. It shows God making a way for Moses to be near him safely.
entries.33:22: When God's glory passes by, he will put Moses in a gap in the rock and cover him with his hand until he has passed. It pictures God protecting Moses from what he could not survive.
entries.33:23: God will then remove his hand, and Moses will see his back, but his face cannot be seen. It means Moses gets a partial, protected glimpse of God, because full sight of God is beyond human ability.
entries.34:1: God tells Moses to cut two new stone tablets to replace the ones he smashed, and promises to write the same words on them again. It shows God gives people a fresh start after failure.
entries.34:2: God tells Moses to be ready in the morning and come up the mountain alone to meet him at the top. It means meeting with God takes preparation and a set time.
entries.34:3: No one else, not even animals, is allowed on the mountain while God meets with Moses. It shows that this meeting with God was holy and set apart.
entries.34:4: Moses did exactly what God said, cutting the stones and climbing the mountain early with them in his hands. It shows obedience to God's instructions, done promptly.
entries.34:5: God came down in a cloud and stood near Moses, and Moses worshiped him. It means God comes close to those who seek him, and the right response is worship.
entries.34:6: God describes himself as compassionate, gracious, patient, and full of faithful love. It means God's basic character toward people is kind and patient.
entries.34:7: God shows mercy to many generations and forgives wrongdoing, yet he does not ignore sin and its effects carry on through families. It means God is forgiving but also takes sin seriously.
entries.34:8: Moses bowed down to the ground in worship right away. It shows his deep respect and gratitude toward God.
entries.34:9: Moses asks God to stay with the people and forgive them, even though they are stubborn, and to make them his own. It means we can honestly admit our faults and still ask God to stay with us.
entries.34:10: God promises to do amazing things for the people that have never been seen before, and everyone will see it. It means God's work in our lives can be something others notice.
entries.34:11: God tells the people to obey his commands and promises to drive out the nations ahead of them. It means obedience and God's help go together.
entries.34:12: God warns them not to make treaties with the people already living in the land, because it would lead them into sin. It means close ties with wrong influences can pull us away from God.
entries.34:13: They are told to tear down the altars, pillars, and idols of those peoples. It means anything set up for false worship had to be removed, not tolerated.
entries.34:14: They must worship no other god, because the Lord will not share his honor with another. It means God expects our loyalty to belong to him alone.
entries.34:15: God warns that making agreements with the local people could lead them to join in their sacrifices and feasts for other gods. It means friendships and alliances can quietly lead us into wrong worship.
entries.34:16: Taking their daughters as wives could lead the sons to worship other gods. It means the people closest to us can shape what we worship.
entries.34:17: They are told not to make metal gods for themselves. It means we should not create our own substitutes for God.
entries.34:18: They must keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread at the set time each year, eating bread without yeast for seven days. It means remembering how God rescued them from Egypt was to be a regular practice.
entries.34:19: Every firstborn male, both of people and animals, belongs to God. It means the first and best of what we have is to be given to God.
entries.34:20: A firstborn donkey could be bought back with a lamb, and every firstborn son had to be bought back; no one comes to God empty-handed. It means coming to God involves giving, not just receiving.
entries.34:21: They work six days but rest on the seventh, even during the busiest farming seasons. It means rest is required, not optional, even when there is much to do.
entries.34:22: They are to celebrate the Feast of Weeks at the first grain harvest and another feast at the end of the year. It means regular times of celebration and thanks to God.
entries.34:23: Three times a year all the men must come before the Lord. It means worship was to be a regular, shared commitment, not a rare event.
entries.34:24: God promises to protect their land and expand it while they go to worship him three times a year. It means trusting God with our time and priorities is safe.
entries.34:25: No yeast may be offered with the blood of the sacrifice, and the Passover offering must not be left until morning. It means worship is to be done God's way, with care and respect.
entries.34:26: They are to bring the firstfruits of their land to God's house and not cook a young goat in its mother's milk. It means giving God the first and best, and following his instructions even in small details.
entries.34:27: God tells Moses to write these words down because the agreement with the people is based on them. It means God's words are meant to be kept and remembered, not just heard.
entries.34:28: Moses stayed with the Lord forty days and nights without eating or drinking and wrote the Ten Commandments on the stones. It means being with God can be so consuming that other needs fade for a time.
entries.34:29: When Moses came down with the stone tablets, his face was shining from being with God, though he didn't know it. It means time with God changes a person in ways others can see.
entries.34:30: Aaron and the people were afraid to come near Moses because his face was shining. It means God's presence can be overwhelming, even when it comes through a person.
entries.34:31: Moses called them back, and Aaron and the leaders came and talked with him. It means leaders have a role in helping people approach God's messenger.
entries.34:32: Afterward all the people came near, and Moses gave them everything the Lord had commanded on the mountain. It means God's instructions are for everyone, not just the leaders.
entries.34:33: When Moses finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face. It means the shining was so intense that it needed covering when he was among the people.
entries.34:34: Whenever Moses went in to talk with the Lord he took the veil off, and when he came out he told the people what God said. It means we should be open before God and honest with others about what he tells us.
entries.34:35: The people saw Moses' face shining, so he covered it again until he went back to the Lord. It means the effect of being with God was visible, and Moses kept returning to God for more.
entries.35:1: Moses gathered the whole nation and told them these were God's own instructions, not his own ideas. It reminds the reader that what follows comes with God's authority and deserves attention.
entries.35:2: Work was allowed for six days, but the seventh day was to be kept as a special day of rest dedicated to God. Anyone who worked on that day was to be executed, showing how seriously God treated this command.
entries.35:3: The people were not even to light a fire in their homes on the Sabbath. This made the day of rest a complete break from ordinary work, even small household tasks.
entries.35:4: Moses passed on to the whole community the command God had given. The instructions that follow were for everyone, not just the leaders.
entries.35:5: People were to bring voluntary gifts to God from what they owned, including gold, silver, and bronze. Giving was to come from a willing heart, not from pressure.
entries.35:6: They were also to bring colored yarns, fine linen, and goat hair. These were the raw materials needed for making the sacred tent and its furnishings.
entries.35:7: Dyed animal skins, leather, and acacia wood were among the materials needed. Ordinary goods from daily life were to be used for God's purposes.
entries.35:8: Olive oil for lamps and spices for the sacred anointing oil and incense were also required. Even small supplies mattered for the worship God had commanded.
entries.35:9: Precious stones were to be given for the priest's special garments and chest piece. Valuable items were to be offered for the honor of God's service.
entries.35:10: Everyone with skill was invited to come and make everything the Lord had commanded. God's work called for both willing givers and willing workers.
entries.35:11: The list begins with the tabernacle itself, its tent, coverings, frames, and bases. These were the parts that made up the portable place of worship.
entries.35:12: The ark, its cover, its carrying poles, and the curtain that screened it were to be made. The ark was the most sacred object, representing God's presence among his people.
entries.35:13: The table for the sacred bread, along with its poles and utensils, was included. This table stood in the holy place and held the bread set before God.
entries.35:14: The lampstand with its lamps and oil was to be made. It provided light in the holy place where the priests served.
entries.35:15: The altar for burning incense, its poles, the anointing oil, the incense, and the curtain for the entrance were also required. Each item served a specific role in worship.
entries.35:16: The altar for burnt offerings, its bronze grating, poles, utensils, and the washing basin with its stand were to be made. These were central to the sacrifices and cleansing of the priests.
entries.35:17: The curtains for the courtyard, its pillars and bases, and the curtain for the courtyard entrance were included. These formed the outer enclosure around the tabernacle.
entries.35:18: The pegs and ropes for the tabernacle and courtyard were also needed. Even the smallest hardware mattered in building God's dwelling place.
entries.35:19: The woven garments for the priests, including Aaron's holy robes and those of his sons, were to be made. These set the priests apart for their service in the holy place.
entries.35:20: After hearing Moses, the people went back to their tents. The next verses show how they responded to what they had been told.
entries.35:21: Everyone whose heart moved them came forward with offerings for the Lord's work. God's work is supported by people who give because they want to, not because they are forced.
entries.35:22: Men and women alike brought gold jewelry as a freewill offering to the Lord. Both genders shared in giving toward God's house.
entries.35:23: Those who owned the needed fabrics, skins, and leather brought them. People gave from whatever materials they already had on hand.
entries.35:24: Those with silver, bronze, or wood brought them as offerings to the Lord. Different people contributed different things, and all of it was needed.
entries.35:25: Skilled women spun yarn with their own hands and brought the finished work. Their practical skills became an offering to God.
entries.35:26: Women with the know-how spun goat hair into cloth. Even less glamorous materials and skills were part of the sacred work.
entries.35:27: The leaders of the community gave the precious stones for the priest's garments. Those with more resources were expected to contribute accordingly.
entries.35:28: They also supplied the spices and oil needed for light, anointing, and incense. The leaders helped cover the ongoing needs of worship.
entries.35:29: Every man and woman who was willing brought freewill offerings for the work God had commanded. The whole community shared in building the place of worship.
entries.35:30: Moses told the people that God had specifically chosen Bezalel from the tribe of Judah. God himself picks the people who will do his work.
entries.35:31: God filled Bezalel with his Spirit and gave him wisdom, understanding, and skill in every kind of craft. God equips people with ability for the tasks he assigns.
entries.35:32: Bezalel was skilled at designing and working with gold, silver, and bronze. His artistic talent was a gift from God to be used for God's purposes.
entries.35:33: He was trained in cutting stones, carving wood, and every kind of craftsmanship. A wide range of practical skills was needed for the tabernacle work.
entries.35:34: God also gave Bezalel and Oholiab the ability to teach others their crafts. Skilled people were expected to pass on their knowledge so the work could be shared.
entries.35:35: God gave them expertise in weaving, designing, and all kinds of skilled work. Their abilities came from God and were to be used fully in his service.
entries.36:1: God gave certain skilled workers the ability and know-how to build the sacred tent, and they were expected to use those gifts to do the work. It means your God-given skills are meant to be put to use for him.
entries.36:2: Moses called together the skilled workers God had gifted and everyone whose heart moved them to help. It shows that God's work is done by people who willingly offer what they have.
entries.36:3: The workers received the people's gifts for building the holy place, and the people kept bringing more every morning. It means generous giving kept the work supplied day after day.
entries.36:4: The skilled workers paused their building to come together. It means they stopped to deal with something important as a group.
entries.36:5: The workers told Moses the people had given far more than the job required. It means the people's generosity had completely covered the need.
entries.36:6: Moses ordered everyone to stop bringing offerings because there was enough. It means wise leadership knows when to say 'that's enough' and stop asking.
entries.36:7: They already had more materials than needed to finish all the work. It means the supply was abundant, not just barely sufficient.
entries.36:8: The skilled craftsmen built the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine linen in blue, purple, and red, decorated with angel figures. It means the place of worship was made with care and beauty.
entries.36:9: Each curtain was the same size, twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide. It means the design was precise and uniform, not random.
entries.36:10: They sewed five curtains into one set and the other five into another set. It means the many pieces were organized into two larger sections.
entries.36:11: They attached blue loops along the outer edge of each set of curtains. It means they prepared the edges so the two sets could be joined.
entries.36:12: Each edge had fifty loops positioned to line up with the loops on the other set. It means the two halves were designed to match perfectly.
entries.36:13: They made fifty gold clasps to connect the two sets, so the tabernacle became one whole. It means the separate parts were joined into a single unified structure.
entries.36:14: They made eleven curtains of goat hair to serve as the tent covering over the tabernacle. It means a sturdy outer layer was added to protect the inner structure.
entries.36:15: Each of these curtains was thirty cubits long and four cubits wide, all identical. It means the covering was made to consistent measurements.
entries.36:16: They joined five curtains into one group and six into another. It means the covering was assembled in two sections, like the inner curtains.
entries.36:17: They put fifty loops on the outer edge of each group of curtains. It means the edges were prepared so the sections could be fastened together.
entries.36:18: They made fifty bronze clasps to join the sections and form the tent. It means the covering was held together as one piece.
entries.36:19: They made a covering of red-dyed sheepskin and another of leather to go over the tent. It means the tabernacle had outer layers for protection from weather.
entries.36:20: They made upright frames of hard wood for the walls of the tabernacle. It means the structure had a solid framework to stand on.
entries.36:21: Each frame was ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. It means the frames were made to exact, matching dimensions.
entries.36:22: Each frame had two pegs set into it, and all the frames were made the same way. It means the parts were standardized so they would fit together.
entries.36:23: They made twenty frames for the south side of the tabernacle. It means the south wall was built from a set number of identical frames.
entries.36:24: They made forty silver bases for the twenty frames, two under each frame to hold its pegs. It means each frame was firmly anchored.
entries.36:25: They made twenty frames for the north side of the tabernacle. It means the north wall matched the south wall in construction.
entries.36:26: They made forty silver bases for these frames, two under each one. It means the north side was anchored the same way as the south.
entries.36:27: They made six frames for the west side, the back of the tabernacle. It means the rear wall was built with fewer frames than the sides.
entries.36:28: They made two extra frames for the corners at the back. It means the corners were given special attention so the structure held together.
entries.36:29: These corner frames were joined at the bottom and top with a single ring, forming both corners. It means the corners were reinforced to keep the walls solid.
entries.36:30: So there were eight frames at the back with sixteen silver bases, two under each frame. It means the rear wall was fully supported.
entries.36:31: They made five wooden rods for the frames on one side of the tabernacle. It means crossbars were added to hold the wall frames steady.
entries.36:32: They made five rods for the other side and five for the back wall on the west. It means every wall had its own set of supporting rods.
entries.36:33: The middle rod ran all the way through the rings from one end to the other. It means one long rod tied the whole structure together.
entries.36:34: They covered the frames with gold, made gold rings for the rods, and covered the rods with gold. It means the structure was made beautiful and precious for God's house.
entries.36:35: They made the inner curtain of fine linen in blue, purple, and red, with angel figures designed by skilled craftsmen. It means a beautiful barrier marked off the most holy area.
entries.36:36: They made four wooden pillars covered with gold, with gold hooks and four silver bases, to hold up the inner curtain. It means the curtain was hung on a sturdy, decorated frame.
entries.36:37: They made a curtain for the entrance of the tent, of fine linen embroidered in blue, purple, and red. It means the doorway was also made with care and beauty.
entries.36:38: They made five pillars with hooks, gold tops and gold bands, and five bronze bases for the entrance curtain. It means the entrance was supported by a strong, decorated frame.
entries.37:1: Bezalel built a wooden chest for the sacred tent, sized about a metre and a quarter long and three-quarters of a metre wide and high. It was the most important piece of furniture in Israel's worship, and God gave exact instructions for it.
entries.37:2: He covered the chest with pure gold inside and out and ran a gold rim around its top edge. The inside mattered as much as the outside, a picture of being clean through and through.
entries.37:3: He cast four gold rings and attached them to the chest's four corners, two on each side. These were the fittings that would let the chest be carried safely.
entries.37:4: He made carrying poles from acacia wood and covered them with gold. Ordinary wood made precious by its covering, ready for a holy job.
entries.37:5: He slid the poles through the rings on the sides of the chest so it could be lifted and carried. The sacred chest was never to be dragged or touched directly, but carried with care.
entries.37:6: He made a solid gold lid for the chest, exactly the same length and width as the chest itself. This lid was where God would meet with his people.
entries.37:7: He hammered out two golden winged figures from a single piece of gold and set them at the two ends of the lid. They were shaped by beating, not casting, showing skilled craftsmanship.
entries.37:8: One winged figure stood at each end of the lid, made as one piece with it. The whole cover was a single unified work of gold.
entries.37:9: The figures' wings spread upward over the lid, and they faced each other with their faces toward the cover. They stood guard over the place where God's presence would rest.
entries.37:10: He built a wooden table about a metre long, half a metre wide and three-quarters of a metre high. This table held the special bread set before God each week.
entries.37:11: He covered the table with pure gold and put a gold rim all around its edge. Even a simple table for bread was made fit for a king's house.
entries.37:12: He added a hand-width border around the table and edged that border with gold. The careful detail shows how seriously God's instructions were taken.
entries.37:13: He made four gold rings and fastened them at the four corners where the table's legs were. These rings were for the carrying poles.
entries.37:14: The rings sat just under the border on the sides, so the poles could slide through and the table could be carried. Everything was designed to be moved without being damaged.
entries.37:15: He made the carrying poles from acacia wood and covered them with gold. Like the chest, the table was carried, not dragged.
entries.37:16: He made all the table's dishes, pans, bowls and jugs from pure gold. The utensils for God's house were the finest available.
entries.37:17: He made the lampstand entirely of pure gold, hammered into shape, with its base, central stem, cups, buds and flowers all one piece. It was a single work of art for giving light in God's house.
entries.37:18: Six branches extended from the lampstand's sides, three on each side. The light would spread out evenly in several directions.
entries.37:19: Each branch had three cups shaped like almond blossoms, each with a bud and a flower. The lampstand was decorated like a flowering tree, a picture of life and light.
entries.37:20: The central stem had four almond-blossom cups, each with its bud and flower. The detail was repeated carefully to match God's design.
entries.37:21: Under each pair of branches there was a bud joined to the stem, for all six branches. The whole lampstand was one connected piece, not parts stuck together.
entries.37:22: The buds and branches were all one piece of pure hammered gold. Nothing was added or bolted on; the whole thing was made as a single work.
entries.37:23: He made seven lamps for the lampstand, plus the small tools for trimming and tending them, all of gold. Even the little tools for keeping the light burning were made precious.
entries.37:24: A whole talent of pure gold, roughly thirty kilograms, went into the lampstand and its tools. It was an expensive piece of furniture, showing how much honour was given to God.
entries.37:25: He made the incense altar from acacia wood, square, about half a metre long and wide and a metre high, with horns at its corners. This was where sweet-smelling incense was burned before God.
entries.37:26: He covered the top, sides and horns with pure gold and put a gold rim around it. Every surface of the altar was made beautiful for its holy use.
entries.37:27: He made two gold rings and fixed them on opposite sides just under the rim, to hold the carrying poles. The altar too was built to be carried safely.
entries.37:28: He made the poles from acacia wood and covered them with gold. The same careful pattern was followed for every piece of furniture.
entries.37:29: He made the sacred anointing oil and the pure sweet-smelling incense, blended by a skilled perfumer. These were set apart for dedicating things to God and for worship that pleased him.
entries.38:1: This describes a large square altar for burnt offerings, made of wood and about seven and a half feet wide and four and a half feet tall. It shows the people built the place of sacrifice exactly as God directed.
entries.38:2: Horns, or raised corners, were added to the altar and the whole thing was covered in bronze. The horns were a sign of strength and protection connected with the altar.
entries.38:3: All the tools used at the altar—baskets, shovels, bowls, hooks, and fire pans—were made of bronze. Everything needed for the altar's work was prepared and ready.
entries.38:4: A bronze grating was placed under the altar's ledge, reaching halfway up. This let air and ashes pass through while the fire burned on top.
entries.38:5: Four rings were made for the corners of the grating so carrying poles could be attached. This made the altar ready to be moved when the people traveled.
entries.38:6: The carrying poles were made of wood and covered with bronze. They were strong and matched the rest of the altar.
entries.38:7: The poles went through the rings on both sides so the altar could be lifted and carried, and the altar itself was hollow inside. It was built to be portable for the journey.
entries.38:8: A bronze basin and stand were made for washing, using bronze mirrors donated by women who served at the entrance of the meeting tent. Their personal items became part of the place of worship.
entries.38:9: The courtyard around the tent was enclosed with fine linen curtains a hundred cubits long on the south side. It created a set-apart space for worship.
entries.38:10: The curtains hung on twenty bronze posts set in bronze bases, with silver hooks and connecting bands. Each part had its proper material and place.
entries.38:11: The north side matched the south, with the same length of curtains on twenty bronze posts and bases, with silver hooks and bands. The courtyard was built evenly and carefully.
entries.38:12: The west side had shorter curtains, fifty cubits long, on ten posts and ten bases with silver bands. The enclosure was completed on every side.
entries.38:13: The east side, where the entrance was, measured fifty cubits across. The opening faced the sunrise.
entries.38:14: On one side of the entrance were curtains fifteen cubits long on three posts and three bases. This formed one half of the gateway area.
entries.38:15: The other side of the entrance matched the first, with fifteen cubits of curtains on three posts and bases. The entrance was balanced on both sides.
entries.38:16: All the curtains around the courtyard were made of the finest linen. The whole enclosure was made with quality material.
entries.38:17: The posts stood on bronze bases, and their tops, hooks, and bands were silver, with silver rings around every post. The courtyard was both sturdy and finely finished.
entries.38:18: The curtain at the courtyard entrance was fine linen embroidered in blue, purple, and red, twenty cubits long and five cubits high, matching the side curtains. The entrance was beautiful and set apart.
entries.38:19: The entrance curtain hung on four posts with bronze bases, and the posts had silver hooks, tops, and bands. Every detail was made as instructed.
entries.38:20: All the tent pegs for the tabernacle and the courtyard were made of bronze. Even the smallest parts were provided for.
entries.38:21: This is the record of the materials used for the tabernacle, the place of witness, counted at Moses' command by the Levites under Ithamar's direction. The work was carefully tracked and accountable.
entries.38:22: Bezalel from the tribe of Judah made everything just as the Lord had commanded Moses. He faithfully carried out God's instructions.
entries.38:23: Working with him was Oholiab from the tribe of Dan, a skilled craftsman and designer in embroidery of blue, purple, red, and fine linen. God gave the work skilled hands to complete it.
entries.38:24: The gold given for the holy place weighed twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels. The people gave generously toward God's house.
entries.38:25: The silver collected from the counted people weighed one hundred talents and one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels. Each person's contribution added up to a large offering.
entries.38:26: Every man twenty years old and older gave a half-shekel, and there were six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty of them. Everyone shared equally in giving.
entries.38:27: One hundred talents of the silver were used for the bases of the sanctuary pillars and the veil, one talent per base. The silver became the foundation of the holy place.
entries.38:28: The remaining silver was used for hooks, tops, and bands for the pillars. Nothing given was wasted.
entries.38:29: The bronze given weighed seventy talents and two thousand four hundred shekels. It was a large offering of metal for the work.
entries.38:30: From the bronze they made the bases for the meeting tent doorway, the bronze altar and its grating, and all the altar's tools. The bronze served the most active parts of worship.
entries.38:31: Bronze was also used for the courtyard bases and its entrance, and for all the pegs of the tabernacle and courtyard. The whole structure was held together with what the people gave.
entries.39:1: Skilled workers made special colored robes for the priests to wear while serving God in the holy place. This shows that God cares about the details of how we approach him in worship.
entries.39:2: The ephod was a special priestly garment made from gold thread and fine colored fabrics. It was made carefully because it was set apart for serving God.
entries.39:3: They hammered gold into thin wire and wove it into the colored cloth. This took great skill and patience, showing that giving God our best work matters.
entries.39:4: They made shoulder straps to connect the front and back of the garment. These practical details kept the sacred clothing held together properly.
entries.39:5: The decorative waistband was made from the same fine materials and matched the rest of the garment. Everything was done exactly as God had instructed Moses.
entries.39:6: They set engraved gemstones into gold settings, with the names of Israel's tribes carved on them. Each tribe was represented before God.
entries.39:7: These stones were attached to the shoulder pieces as a reminder of the people of Israel before God. The priest carried the whole nation with him when he served.
entries.39:8: The chestpiece was made with the same fine materials and design as the ephod. It was a beautiful and unified part of the priest's outfit.
entries.39:9: The chestpiece was folded double into a square about the size of a hand span. Its simple shape held deep meaning for the priest's role.
entries.39:10: Four rows of precious stones were mounted on the chestpiece, starting with carnelian, chrysolite, and emerald. These costly stones showed how precious God's people are to him.
entries.39:11: The second row held a ruby, a sapphire, and an onyx. Each stone was carefully chosen and set in place.
entries.39:12: The third row contained a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst. The variety of stones reflected the variety among God's people.
entries.39:13: The fourth row had a topaz, a beryl, and a jasper, all set in gold. Every stone was secured with care and craftsmanship.
entries.39:14: There were twelve stones, one for each tribe, each engraved with a tribe's name. The priest represented all twelve tribes equally before God.
entries.39:15: They made twisted gold chains for the chestpiece. These chains connected the sacred pieces together securely.
entries.39:16: They made gold settings and rings and attached the rings to the ends of the chestpiece. These fittings kept the chestpiece in its proper place.
entries.39:17: The twisted chains were fastened to the rings at the ends of the chestpiece. This connected the chestpiece to the rest of the priest's garment.
entries.39:18: The other ends of the chains were attached to the front of the ephod at the shoulder pieces. This held the chestpiece firmly against the priest's chest.
entries.39:19: They made two more gold rings and placed them on the lower inner edge of the chestpiece. These rings faced the ephod to keep everything aligned.
entries.39:20: Two more gold rings were placed on the front of the ephod near the shoulder join and above the waistband. These matched the rings on the chestpiece.
entries.39:21: A blue cord tied the rings together so the chestpiece would stay in place and not come loose. This was done exactly as God had commanded Moses.
entries.39:22: The robe worn under the ephod was made entirely of blue cloth. Blue was a color associated with what is holy and set apart.
entries.39:23: The robe had a reinforced opening at the top for the head, like a soldier's collar. This practical detail kept the garment from tearing.
entries.39:24: Pomegranate-shaped decorations in blue, purple, and red were woven around the hem of the robe. These added beauty and meaning to the priest's clothing.
entries.39:25: Gold bells were placed between the pomegranates all around the hem. The bells would sound as the priest moved, marking his service before God.
entries.39:26: Bells and pomegranates alternated around the hem of the robe. This pattern was made just as God had instructed Moses.
entries.39:27: They made tunics of fine linen for Aaron and his sons. The priests wore clean, well-made clothing for their service.
entries.39:28: They made the turban, head coverings, and linen undergarments with care. Every piece of the priest's clothing was made to honor God.
entries.39:29: The sash was made of fine linen with colorful embroidery. It was made exactly as God had commanded Moses.
entries.39:30: They made a gold plate for the turban and engraved on it the words 'Holy to the LORD.' This declared that the priest belonged entirely to God.
entries.39:31: The gold plate was tied to the turban with a blue cord. This was done just as God had instructed Moses.
entries.39:32: All the work on the tent of meeting was finished, and the people had done everything exactly as God commanded. Obedience to God's instructions was complete.
entries.39:33: They brought the completed tent and all its parts to Moses. Everything was assembled and presented for inspection.
entries.39:34: They brought the outer coverings of dyed sheepskin and leather, along with the curtain for the entrance. These protected and enclosed the holy place.
entries.39:35: They brought the ark of the law with its carrying poles and its cover. The ark was the most sacred object, holding God's covenant.
entries.39:36: They brought the table with all its utensils and the special bread set before God. These items were used in worship and offering.
entries.39:37: They brought the lampstand with its lamps and utensils and the oil for lighting it. This provided light for the holy place.
entries.39:38: They brought the gold altar, the holy oil, the sweet-smelling incense, and the curtain for the tent entrance. These were all used in worship and sacrifice.
entries.39:39: They brought the bronze altar with its grating, poles, and utensils, plus the washing basin and its stand. These were used for sacrifices and cleansing.
entries.39:40: They brought the courtyard curtains, pillars, bases, entrance curtain, cords, pegs, and all the equipment needed for the tent of meeting. Every item for worship was ready.
entries.39:41: These were the special clothes made for worship in the sacred tent, including the outfits the priests wore while serving. It reminds the reader that approaching God was treated with care and respect.
entries.39:42: The people carried out every instruction the Lord had given through Moses, down to the details. It shows that faithful obedience means doing what God asks, not just the parts we like.
entries.39:43: Moses inspected all the work and saw it matched exactly what the Lord had commanded, so he blessed the people. It means God notices careful, complete obedience and responds with blessing.
entries.40:1: God speaks directly to Moses here, giving him the next set of instructions. It reminds the reader that God guides his people step by step rather than leaving them to guess.
entries.40:2: God tells Moses to set up the sacred tent on the first day of the new year. This marks a fresh start, showing that worship of God stands at the beginning of Israel's new year.
entries.40:3: Inside the tent, the chest holding God's law was to be placed and screened off by a curtain. This taught that God's word is central and that access to his presence is carefully ordered.
entries.40:4: The table for the sacred bread and the lampstand were to be set up with everything arranged properly, and the lamps kept burning. It shows that worship involves careful order and ongoing devotion, not just occasional effort.
entries.40:5: The gold altar for burning incense was placed just outside the inner curtain, and a curtain hung at the tent's entrance. This arranged the space so that prayer and approach to God had their proper place.
entries.40:6: The large altar for animal sacrifices stood at the entrance of the tent. It reminded the people that coming near to God required sacrifice from the very doorway.
entries.40:7: A basin filled with water was placed between the tent and the altar. It was there for washing, teaching that those who approach God must be cleansed.
entries.40:8: Moses was to set up the courtyard curtains all around and hang a curtain at its entrance. This made a clear boundary around the holy space, marking it off from ordinary life.
entries.40:9: Moses was to anoint the tent and everything in it with holy oil, setting it apart for God. It shows that things used in worship are dedicated specially to him.
entries.40:10: The altar of sacrifice and its equipment were also to be anointed and made most holy. This underlined that the place of sacrifice was especially set apart for God's purposes.
entries.40:11: The washing basin and its stand were anointed too, making them holy. Even the simple tools of cleansing were dedicated to God's service.
entries.40:12: Aaron and his sons were to come to the tent entrance and be washed with water. This showed that those who serve God must first be cleansed before they begin.
entries.40:13: Aaron was to be dressed in the holy robes and anointed so he could serve as priest. It shows that the role of priest was a gift and calling from God, not something taken on oneself.
entries.40:14: Aaron's sons were also brought forward and dressed in their coats. The whole family was included in the service, showing that God's calling extends to a household.
entries.40:15: The sons were anointed just as their father was, making their priesthood permanent for future generations. It shows that God intended a lasting line of priests to serve his people.
entries.40:16: Moses did everything exactly as the Lord commanded him. This sets an example of full obedience to God's instructions, down to the details.
entries.40:17: The tent was actually set up on the first day of the first month in the second year. This gives a real date, showing that God's instructions were carried out in history, not just in theory.
entries.40:18: Moses set up the structure piece by piece, laying the bases and standing up the frames and posts. It shows that building a place for God took patient, careful work.
entries.40:19: He spread the outer coverings over the tent just as God had ordered. Obedience in the small, practical details mattered.
entries.40:20: Moses placed the law inside the chest, added the carrying poles, and put the cover on top. The law at the heart of the chest shows that God's word was the center of Israel's worship.
entries.40:21: He brought the chest into the tent and hung the curtain in front of it, exactly as commanded. This kept the most holy place set apart and honored God's instructions.
entries.40:22: The table was placed in the tent on the north side, outside the inner curtain. Each item had its assigned place, showing order in worship.
entries.40:23: Moses arranged the bread on the table before the Lord as God had said. This was a regular act of devotion, acknowledging God's presence and provision.
entries.40:24: The lampstand was set opposite the table on the south side of the tent. The layout kept the space balanced and orderly for worship.
entries.40:25: Moses lit the lamps before the Lord, just as he had been commanded. Light in the holy place symbolized God's presence and guidance.
entries.40:26: The gold altar was placed inside the tent, in front of the inner curtain. This positioned prayer and incense close to the place of God's presence.
entries.40:27: Moses burned sweet-smelling incense on it, as the Lord had ordered. The pleasant smoke pictured prayers rising to God.
entries.40:28: He hung the curtain at the doorway of the tent. This completed the entrance, keeping the holy space properly enclosed.
entries.40:29: Moses set the altar of sacrifice at the tent entrance and offered the burnt and grain offerings on it, as commanded. Sacrifice stood at the doorway, showing that approach to God begins with offering.
entries.40:30: The water basin was placed between the altar and the tent for washing. It stood ready for the cleansing that worship required.
entries.40:31: Moses, Aaron, and Aaron's sons washed their hands and feet in it. Even the leader and the priests needed cleansing before serving God.
entries.40:32: They washed whenever they entered the tent or came near the altar, just as God had ordered Moses. This made cleansing a regular habit, not a one-time event.
entries.40:33: Moses finished the courtyard curtains and the entrance curtain, completing the whole work. The account ends with the project fully done, showing faithful follow-through.
entries.40:34: The cloud covered the tent and the Lord's glory filled the house. This was God's visible sign that he had come to dwell among his people and accepted their work.
entries.40:35: Moses could not enter the tent because the cloud rested on it and God's glory filled it. God's presence was so overwhelming that even Moses had to stay outside.
entries.40:36: Whenever the cloud lifted from the tent, the Israelites set out on their journey. God himself directed their travel, so they moved only when he led.
entries.40:37: While the cloud stayed put, the people stayed put and did not move until it lifted. This taught them patience and dependence on God's timing.
entries.40:38: The Lord's cloud rested on the tent by day and fire was in it by night, visible to all Israel throughout their journeys. God's presence stayed with his people constantly, guiding and reassuring them day and night.
